title.rendered: we come to collect: a flirtation, with capitalism

content.rendered:
By David Walters

In, we come to collect: a flirtation, with capitalism, performers Jennifer Kidwell and Bandon Kazen-Maddox have ultimately not come to collect at all. Instead, they have come to give. Give big and wholeheartedly. Give personally and with love. Come to present a mirror unto ourselves that reflects back our joys and heartaches, laughter and tears, fears and foibles.

To have a play (which it’s really not as much as it is a performance installation) make you laugh, make you think, make you consider the decisions and choices that you’ve made in your life, all in the space of a little over an hour and a half, is extra-ordinary. As they say during the course of the evening, this presentation is not about them, but about us, the ones sitting in the seats, and they are but mere facilitators.

The set is a lush drawing room, heavily curtained, chandelier dangling stage right, a large mirror that doubles as a projection screen against the back wall reflecting the anticipatory audience, and a settee. Upon the settee reclines ASL signed language artist, Bandon Kazen-Maddox. Sitting on the end, facing the mirror, is our main guide for the evening, Jennifer Kidwell. They both present a surety in themselves and enjoy playing together that quickly wins the audience over and allows us to, with only a little trepidation, put ourselves completely at their disposal. This trust that is quickly built up permits them to take us on the wild ride that is the evening.

There are several moments of revealing audience participation that bring us further into the themes of time, self-love, race, money, work, the lies we tell ourselves, and Mardi Gras. All of that mayhem is mixed up together and held firmly in place by honest laughter, which is the true artistry of this piece.

Through the chuckles and guffaws, you will feel discomfort at times, be challenged to examine the you that you think you are, and encouraged to believe the one true fact that you are an absolute miracle, even if your ultimate fate is death by Mardi Gras.

A truly fun and thought-provoking evening.

——

we come to collect: a flirtation, with capitalism at The Flea Theater, 20 Thomas Street, NYC, through Saturday, September 27 only.

Written, directed, and performed by Jennifer Kidwell, with ASL artist and performer Brandon Kazen-Maddox. Co-directed by Adam Lazarus.

Scenic Design by Jian Jung, Lighting Design by Evan Spigelman, Sound Design by Jordan McCree, Video Design by Matthew Deinhart, and Props and objects designed by Petra Floyd.

Tickets, $25-$48, can be gotten HERE.

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

title.rendered: GUEST CONTRIBUTION – ZaZa Flamenca and Gabriel Hermida in Chansons & Tango at Pangea

content.rendered:
By Paul Meltzer

Pangea” is what scientists call the one big merged landmass that existed before it all broke up into continents and drifted around the globe.  Fitting then that Pangea, the storied East Village venue that performance artist Joey Arias once called “the downtown Carlyle”, would be the setting for an evening bringing together French chansons and Argentinian tango in one elegant, if slightly daffy, intimate room.  When the lights are low and we are in ZaZa’s hands, even the glittery animal art seems to make sense.

ZaZa Flamenca and Gabriel Hermida  are clearly both remarkable talents.  Gabriel plucks his guitar strings with force, fervor and panache, as much Django as tango.  Zaza is such an appealing presence, so comfortable with the audience and as canny and charming as could be in her satiny red dress and wavy locks.  Then she opens her clear, buttery smooth voice.  With her sensitive, unfailingly tasteful phrasing, listening to her is like sipping well-chosen wine (French, of course).  From Edith Piaf to Jacques Brel and masters of tango less familiar to American audiences, her song choices are all pleasing, too.

Their banter is entertaining and we do get glimpses of the worlds they proudly bring with them.  Could the evening be even better?  They could use a director.  It would be nice if it felt like we were on a progression–a feeling of beginning, middle, and end.  The elements were all there, including getting to know them, and it was nice and casual and real.  But keeping all those qualities, it could be nudged into more of a cabaret show–“Transporting you from Paris to Buenos Aires…all in one unforgettable night” as the billing goes–more than just a very high quality cabaret set.

And as wonderful and winning as ZaZa is, she executes the songs so tastefully yet never really seems to go to a vulnerable place, sharing her feelings through the music.  She tells us she studied method acting for a while in New York.  This is a good impulse.  As an HB Studio teacher once said, “If you don’t feel anything, they won’t feel anything.”

Many artists seem to find the idea of being emotionally vulnerable kind of embarrassing, especially when they have the option of just looking great and being delightful and appealing.  But that openness–authentically and vulnerably “going there” however quietly–can really bond artist and audience and take the whole experience to the next level.

Don’t get me wrong.  It was all lovely, and the audience roared approval.  As we were taking care of the check, a lady from the other side of the room came over to snap a picture of the–was it a zebra?–over our table.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Leading Ladies: A Celebration Through the Decades

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“You can build me up, you can tear me down
You can try but I’m unbreakable”

Just over a dozen performers–some returning to the 54 Below stage, others making their 54 Below debut–enter into the venue of 54 Below. This intimate, dimly-lit room is immediately embraced with one of the most supportive, engaged audiences I have seen in a cabaret space for quite some time.

Leading Ladies: A Celebration Through the Decades, produced by Carly Sesti, was a performance of exactly that: not only did thirteen talented and vocally diverse singers take the stage—individually, as duets, and as together as a whole—but their powerhouse vocals carried us across the powerful women whose voices have stamped musical theater. From the Golden Age, to today’s modern theater, this group showcased the lyrics that we all recognize, sing along with, and listen to on repeat. Selections from musicals such as Cabaret, SIX, The Color Purple, Waitress, Wicked, and Ragtime were just a few heard this evening. These leading ladies brought their own power and personal renditions to each performance. I appreciated the range of numbers–“Your Daddy’s Son,” sang by Kellie Williams; “Cabaret,” from Allison Calabrese; “I’m Here,” performed by Aliya Gardner; “She Used to Be Mine,” performed by Talitha McDougall Jones, and a handful of standout numbers performed by commanding vocalist, Liz Davis.

There was a presence of such uplifting, electric energy in 54 Below, as the first duet took the stage with “Suddenly Seymour,” kicking off a flow of impressive performances. The theme of women’s strength, endurance, deep commitment to love, and overcoming the obstacles–and men–that have tried tearing us down was profound and felt this evening.

“She is broken and won’t ask for help
She is messy, but she’s kind
She is lonely most of the time
She is all of this mixed up
And baked in a beautiful pie
She is gone, but she used to be mine”

I am always grateful to spend an evening in this venue, and this Tuesday-night cabaret was no exception. In just under 75 minutes, we enjoyed a treat of iconic songs we may not have heard for some time, meshed with those we can’t go a few days without hearing someone belting out–whether we live within or outside the world of musical. Concluding with an electrifying “Defying Gravity,” the group of performers left me wanting to hear more from each of them. Each one of them took the stage with presence and commanded the room’s attention, the way that the original legends had when they had taken stages across this city not so long ago.

 

Produced by Carly Sesti.

FEATURING: Brian Ashton, Nicholas Barnes, Allison Calabrese, Liz Davis, Tiara Fielding, Kaileigh Fiorillo, Kelly C Fox, Aliya Gardner, Amy Herzberg, Talitha McDougall Jones, Zibby Nolting, Carly Sesti, and Kellie Williams.

Joined by Frank Sanchez on piano.

Tickets for upcoming shows at 54 Below, 254 W 54th St. Cellar, NYC 10019, can be purchased here, or you can call (646) 476-3551.

title.rendered: Stravinsky’s Timeless Fable Reborn on Shelter Island

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

What emerges when musical theater’s most intimate devils meet Stravinsky’s most deceptive angel? What happens when this encounter unfolds in the loving embrace of a community that understands, perhaps better than most Manhattan venues, that great art requires not grandeur but truth?

On a sultry August evening in the Shelter Island School Auditorium, something extraordinary transpired. Here, under the auspices of the Shelter Island Friends of Music, David Bernard and his magnificent Park Avenue Chamber Symphony presented Stravinsky’s L’histoire du Soldat with such luminous artistry that the work’s century-old themes felt urgently, achingly contemporary.

The Devil’s Bargain: Context and Creation

The Soldier’s Tale emerged from Stravinsky’s own pact with necessity. Stranded in wartime Switzerland, financially desperate, and cut off from his usual Russian and Parisian networks, the composer conceived this chamber work as touring entertainment. This piece could survive on sheer creative wit rather than orchestral opulence. The 1918 influenza pandemic ultimately scuttled Stravinsky’s modest touring dreams, much as our own recent pandemic reminded us of art’s simultaneously fragile and essential natures.

From these constraints emerged what many consider Stravinsky’s most perfectly integrated theatrical work—a piece that represents “a complete change of paradigm” following the horrors of the Great War. The work’s seven-instrument ensemble, deliberately modeled on American jazz bands while filtered through Stravinsky’s revolutionary harmonic language, created something entirely unprecedented in classical music.

Most significantly, The Soldier’s Tale “straddles the divide between the competing ideals of reversion to traditionalism and the rejection of tradition.” The work’s “Grand Chorale” recalls Bach’s harmonic procedures, albeit with modern dissonances. In contrast, the “Dance du Diable” and the “Triumphal March” recall the grotesque aggression of The Rite, with their use of the extreme registers of each instrument, their unrelenting dissonance, and their abandonment of tradition.

A scene from A Soldier’s Tale performed by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Maestro Bernard’s Revelatory Leadership: Navigating Stravinsky’s Technical Labyrinth

Under David Bernard’s direction, the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony musicians made familiar music sound freshly minted while conquering some of the most demanding challenges in the chamber music repertoire. Bernard’s interpretation revealed why Gramophone magazine has praised his recordings for their “intensity, spontaneity, propulsive rhythm, textural clarity, dynamic control, and well-judged phrasing.” His approach to Stravinsky’s challenging score demonstrated the same “dramatic and incisive conducting” that has earned him recognition across four continents.

The technical demands of The Soldier’s Tale are formidable. Stravinsky’s score reveals his chief technical traits: bitonality (two voices, each in different keys), rhythmic disruption, dislocation and asymmetry, as well as the telltale prevalence of a diversity of short motifs repeated in layered ostinati. These polytonal structures, where competing pitch centers create harmonic tension without resolution, require musicians to maintain absolute intonational integrity while navigating constantly shifting metrical terrain.

Álfheiður Sæmundsson’s violin performance proved particularly masterful in confronting the instrument’s central dramatic burden. Her violin must serve as the lynchpin of the entire drama: the soldier’s violin (complete with little cadenza), a metaphor for the soul that he will ultimately lose. The technical challenges include exposed solo cadenzas and the need to maintain perfect intonational accuracy while navigating Stravinsky’s bitonal harmonic structures—particularly treacherous in the “Little Concert” section, where the violin establishes precise tuning relationships with the other instruments.

Trent Firestine appears as the Devil in a scene from A Soldier’s Tale performed by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Alex Yu‘s clarinet work demonstrated exceptional command of some of Stravinsky’s most demanding woodwind writing. The clarinet’s role requires absolute rhythmic precision, particularly through Stravinsky’s constant meter changes, while maintaining the jazz influences Stravinsky absorbed from written scores rather than live performances. Yu’s performance in the crucial “Pastorale” movement, where the particular challenge of intonation with the clarinet, achieved a delicate balance between technical accuracy and expressive musicality.

James Marshall’s bassoon playing navigated some of the instrument’s most treacherous passages in the repertoire. The “Pastorale” movement presents specific intonational challenges requiring ultra-careful listening and flexing to match the clarinet, while the “Ragtime” movement—with its tempo marking of 192 to the eighth and constant meter changes can easily become what is sometimes called a “‘ragged’ ragtime.” Marshall’s performance demonstrated the technical mastery required to execute extensive passages involving only two notes, high F# and high G#, while maintaining perfect ensemble coordination.

Mario Correa’s trumpet work exemplified the brass challenges inherent in Stravinsky’s jazz-influenced writing. The score’s demands include not only the technical precision required for the rhythmically complex passages but also the stylistic authenticity needed to evoke the tango, waltz, and ragtime idioms that Stravinsky, despite never having heard jazz performed live, incorporated into his harmonic language.

Trent Firestine as the Devil. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Bruce Leggett-Flynn: A Tour de Force of Theatrical Virtuosity

The evening’s revelation was undoubtedly Bruce Leggett-Flynn, whose solo inhabitation of every speaking role—Narrator, Soldier, Devil, and all the Devil’s various disguises—proved nothing short of miraculous. This British actor, whose background spans rugby fields and nightclub stages, brought a specificity and theatrical intelligence to each character that illuminated every corner of Ramuz’s text.

Leggett-Flynn’s Devil was particularly memorable—not the cartoonish tempter of lesser productions, but rather a figure of genuine menace wrapped in seductive charm. His transitions between characters occurred with such seamless artistry that the audience never questioned the theatrical logic of his multiple personas. His final incarnation as the triumphant Devil possessed a chilling inevitability that left the audience contemplating the work’s moral complexities long after the final notes faded.

Visual Splendor: Ariel Adkins’ Surrealist Revolution

Ariel Adkins‘ production design proved a master class in theatrical imagination. As the founder of Artfully Awear, Adkins has spent years transforming clothing into storytelling tools. Her work has been featured in The New York Times, Vogue, and Forbes through collaborations with MoMA, the Guggenheim, and other significant cultural institutions worldwide.

Her surrealist-inspired design concept—layers of translucent chiffon serving as both sculptural environment and projection surface—created a visual language perfectly aligned with Stravinsky’s musical modernism. The costumes’ emphasis on “illusion and fragmentation” echoed not only the composer’s ties to Surrealism but also the work’s central themes of identity and transformation. Adkins possesses that rare ability to make art more accessible” through visual storytelling—precisely what this production achieved.

Bruce Leggett-Flynn as the narrator in a scene from A Soldier’s Tale performed by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

The Musical Revelation: Seven Players, Infinite Worlds—Stravinsky’s Polytonal Architecture

The heart of this performance lay in Bernard’s conducting and his musicians’ responses to Stravinsky’s revolutionary harmonic language. The work’s instrumentation creates equal players in the drama—each instrumentalist becomes a character rather than a mere accompanist. What makes this particularly challenging is Stravinsky’s use of bi-quintal structures, where two perfect fifth intervals are stabilized and elaborated, creating harmonic tensions between competing pitch centers that require absolute precision from each performer.

Paul Robertson’s percussion work proved central to the drama’s psychological architecture. Arguably, the percussion has the last word in the whole piece, representing the Devil’s ultimate triumph. The technical challenges include navigating multiple editions of the percussion part, as there are differences between each edition, even those approved by Stravinsky, while maintaining the specific timbral colors Stravinsky demanded for his jazz-influenced rhythmic structures.

Ed Matin‘s trombone and Bill Nealon‘s double bass provided the harmonic foundation for Stravinsky’s bitonal experiments. The double bass faces challenges in the work’s use of layered ostinati, which create an iridescent equilibrium—repetitive patterns that must remain rhythmically absolute while supporting the harmonic tensions of Stravinsky’s competing tonal centers.

The ensemble’s mastery of Stravinsky’s metrical complexities proved particularly impressive. The work is rife with changing time signatures, demanding rock-solid steadiness from each player to prevent the ensemble from derailing. The famous “Ragtime” movement presents the ultimate test—a tempo marking of 192 to the eighth note combined with constant meter changes that can destroy lesser ensembles.

Bernard’s approach to ensemble building creates immersive music-making that engages contemporary audiences in uniquely meaningful ways. This evening’s performance demonstrated precisely why the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony has earned such critical acclaim for transforming classical music experiences through technical mastery wedded to interpretive insight.

A scene from A Soldier’s Tale performed by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Movement, Magic, and Meaning

The contributions of the movement ensemble—Trent Firestine, Ariel Adkins, and nine-year-old Natali Leon—added layers of physical poetry to the musical storytelling. Their presence reminded us that Stravinsky conceived this work as a multimedia theater piece, not concert music with incidental staging.

Young Natali Leon’s participation particularly moved the audience, suggesting that great art crosses generational boundaries when presented with authentic artistic commitment. Her involvement embodied the Shelter Island Friends of Music‘s mission to bring “world-renowned artists and rising stars” together in the service of musical excellence.

Technical Excellence in Service of Art

The production team’s contributions proved equally essential. John Kaasik’s lighting design created atmospheric support that enhanced rather than overwhelmed the intimate scale. At the same time, James Marshall’s direction demonstrated the sophisticated understanding of musical theater that comes from deep experience in both music and drama. Sara Mundy’s stage management ensured seamless transitions that maintained the work’s essential flow and continuity.

Trent Firestine as the Devil. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

The Deeper Resonances: Why This Soldier’s Tale Matters Now

What made this performance extraordinary was its recognition that The Soldier’s Tale speaks directly to our contemporary moment. Stravinsky’s Faustian tale about a soldier who trades his authentic self for material success resonates with poignancy in our age of digital distraction and commodified culture.

The work’s themes of exile, displacement, and the search for authentic human connection resonate powerfully with audiences still processing their own recent experiences of isolation and loss. I propose that the most meaningful artistic experiences often emerge when performers and audiences recognize their shared humanity through the transformative power of great art.

A Community Triumph

This performance exemplified everything that makes Shelter Island Friends of Music such a vital cultural institution. Their commitment to presenting “world-class cultural performances, free of charge” creates precisely the kind of community-centered artmaking that nurtures both artists and audiences. Their partnership with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony demonstrates how musical excellence and community engagement can coexist beautifully.

The Front Row Center has documented that the most memorable musical experiences often occur when “modern life meets a gentler, more connected past”—precisely what transpired in this intimate school auditorium setting.

The Lasting Impact

As the final notes of the “Triumphal March of the Devil” faded and the audience erupted in applause, one sensed that something genuinely special had occurred. This was not merely a successful performance of a challenging work, but rather a reminder of why live music-making remains irreplaceable in our increasingly digital world.

David Bernard’s vision of classical music as accessible, immediate, and emotionally transformative found perfect expression in this evening’s artmaking. His innovative approaches to audience engagement—evidenced throughout the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s 25-year history—continue to demonstrate that traditional concert formats need not be abandoned, but rather reimagined with greater humanity and artistic integrity.

The Soldier’s Tale, Courtesy PACS

The Art of Necessary Magic

This Soldier’s Tale succeeded because everyone involved understood that Stravinsky’s masterpiece demands not just musical competence but theatrical courage and emotional truthfulness. Opening Night Online has observed that the most remarkable performances achieve that rare synthesis where technical mastery serves emotional authenticity—where tradition and innovation coexist without contradiction.

On this August evening, Bruce Leggett-Flynn, Ariel Adkins, David Bernard, and the extraordinary musicians of the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony reminded us why live performance remains essential: it creates shared experiences that no recording, however excellent, can replicate.

They demonstrated that the most profound art often emerges not from abundance but from constraint—from artists who understand that limitations can become sources of creative liberation. They proved that community-based artmaking, when approached with appropriate seriousness and love, can achieve the highest levels of artistic excellence.

Shelter Island Friends of Music and institutions like it represent something precious in our cultural landscape: spaces where art serves community and community nurtures art, where professional excellence meets human warmth, and where the transformative power of great music can touch hearts and change lives. For those fortunate enough to witness this Soldier’s Tale, the memory will linger like the best kind of devil’s bargain—one where the exchange enriched rather than impoverished the soul, where art’s ancient magic proved once again its capacity to make us more fully human.

It is worth noting that James Marshall, who served as both director and principal bassoonist for this production, brings a unique perspective as a resident of Shelter Island. His dual role—guiding the theatrical vision while navigating the formidable technical challenges of Stravinsky’s bassoon writing—exemplifies an artistic versatility that makes community-based music-making so vital to our cultural landscape.

Trent Firestine in a scene from A Soldier’s Tale performed by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

Maestro Bernard’s Illuminating Post-Concert Discourse

Following the performance, David Bernard offered the audience an illuminating post-concert discussion revealing the philosophical currents of Stravinsky’s masterpiece. Speaking to an attentive gathering of music lovers, Bernard explored how the composer’s revolutionary approach to form and harmony creates what he termed “musical realism”—art that reflects life as it truly is, rather than as we might wish it to be.

“Stravinsky’s genius,” Bernard explained, “lies in his combination of traditional forms—marches, even Bach chorales—with dissonance and irregular meters to create a full picture of depth and realism.” This approach, he noted, stands in stark contrast to classical music’s tendency to deliver “an aural picture of an idealized world.” Instead, Stravinsky gives us life unvarnished, much as Picasso’s visual abstractions distort familiar forms to reveal more profound truths about human experience.

Bernard’s analysis proved particularly insightful regarding the work’s use of chorales as “points of introspection where the underlying meaning is revealed.” These sections employ the familiar forms of Bach chorales to create moments of reflection that contrast sharply with the everyday urgency of the marches. Yet even in these contemplative passages, Stravinsky’s incorporation of dissonance ensures that we remain grounded in the real world rather than ascending to some ethereal realm of pure beauty.

Maestro David Bernard leading a post-concert discussion on Stravinsky and his Soldier’s Tale. Photo by Adam Bundy Photography

The evening’s most fascinating revelation concerned the work’s controversial final percussion coda. Bernard posed the central interpretive question that has divided performers and scholars for decades: Should the ending utilize a crescendo or a decrescendo? While Stravinsky explicitly indicated a decrescendo—”essentially a slow extinguishing of light indicating the soldier’s loss”—many performers have chosen a crescendo to emphasize the Devil’s triumph. This interpretive choice, Bernard suggested, fundamentally alters the work’s meaning, transforming a meditation on human frailty into a celebration of evil’s victory.

The discussion illuminated not only Stravinsky’s compositional philosophy but the broader questions that make The Soldier’s Tale enduringly relevant. In an age when traditional certainties seem increasingly fragile, the work’s unflinching examination of moral compromise and spiritual loss resonates with particular urgency.

Stravinsky’s Timeless Fable Reborn on Shelter Island

The Artists

Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

David Bernard — Conductor
Álfheiður Sæmundsson — Violin
Alex Yu — Clarinet

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

Octet is a musical in song-cycle form. The musical takes us into a support group for technology addicts, walking us through the eight group members’ individual struggles with technology. From gaming addiction to conspiracy theories, the show pokes at all the beasts that hide in our phones. Sitting in a circle in a dimly lit basement, the actors nail the balancing act that comes with being uncomfortable in a setting but desperately wanting the help that that place can provide.

First, the good: Chilling. Harrowing. The music in Octet is out of this world. This is music that I want to listen to over and over on repeat. The hymns, which started and ended the show, were rich. Like a cocoon, they were warm and enveloping. “The Forest” and “Monster” are two examples. “Candy” is another fantastic song–bright, uplifting. “Beautiful” is light and a fantastic way to bring the show to a close. Other songs, while equally well written and musically stunning, were confusing–like “Little God.” The songs spanned a range of genres, providing a fantastic amount of variety.

Now, the plot: There were moments of incredible depth and joy. However, overall, there were lots of moments of confusion. It was unclear what story this show was trying to tell. Yes, phones are bad—isolating, addicting. But what is the message of the show? This show tried to fit everyone’s story in, everyone’s tales of addiction and online encounters gone wrong. But, ultimately, it left us with a lot of depiction but without much conviction or agency. Do we throw our phones away? Is moderation possible? Do we focus on the good? What do we do?! Of course, it’s a massive question, but I was really hoping the show would give some kind of answer.

There were great moments of storytelling. The depiction of a train–with everyone glued to their phone–resonated with a sickening kind of aftertaste. The coffee break was fantastic–the soul-baring emotion of the songs relegated to awkward eye contact and oversharing, the menace of a stark line between “too much” and “not enough” and a complete inability to know where to stand, how, when, and why. Technology has shaped our relationships and ability to connect in, mostly, devastating ways. This is absolutely a show for the moment. It’s timely and feels fresh.

I hope this show clarifies the story and, especially, its message. Because wow! The music is fantastic. I hope this show goes far!

Music, Lyrics, Book and Vocal Arrangements: Dave Malloy

Director: Amanda Dehnert

content.rendered:
By Victoria Lynne Dammer

Ballet is magical, taking you on a journey that treats your sight and hearing to an elevated state of pure euphoria. Hong Kong Ballet, presenting The Butterfly Lovers at the David H. Koch Theater at Lincoln Center, transfixed the audience on a higher plane.

The performance was stunning. The New York City Ballet Orchestra, with guest conductor LIO Kuokman, performed the musical score that reverberated throughout the concert hall.

Hong Kong Ballet, an internationally recognized world-class troupe of dancers from around the globe, was formed in 1979 and has been delighting audiences since its inception. Presently, they perform works by Artistic Director Septime Webre with today’s finest choreographers, such as Christopher Wheeldon and Annabelle Lopez Ochoa. HU Song Wei Ricky and Libretto and Associate choreographer MAI Jingwen choreographed The Butterfly Lovers.

The story of star-crossed lovers is well-known, with some love affairs ending happily and others with sad endings that leave the audience in tears. The Butterfly Lovers is the latter, or is it?

Zhu Yintai (Xuan CHENG or YE Feifei) is trapped inside her parents’ mansion, curious about the outside world but forbidden to experience its wonders. Her father relents, allowing Zhu to leave home to study. On her way to the academy, she encounters Liang Shanbo (MA Renjie or Ryo KATO). Zhu and Liang become secret lovers, and their love is fulfilled in a dream. The scene is sensuous; their commitment is so strong that they cannot bear to be away from each other.

Zhu’s parents have planned an arranged marriage for her, and her mother changes the course of the two lovers. The outcome is not as one would wish.

The ballet dancers and danseurs were garbed in traditional Hanfu attire, floor-length flowing costumes, with crimson and billowing white shirts underneath, which floated like butterflies as they performed their dances.

Ballerinas danced in traditional white sparkling tutus during one scene. Danseurs with bluish grey Hanfu attire with black accents displayed their extraordinary physicality. Zhu’s mother dressed her in conventional red wedding garments for the wedding she planned. She was unaware of the cost of the interference to her, her daughter, and her lover Liang.

The Butterfly Lovers will transfix you for two hours, and the limited four performance run is too short for this exceptional production.

Hong Kong Ballet presents The Butterfly Lovers at the David H. Koch Theater at Lincoln Center. Concept and choreography by HU Song Wei Ricky and Libretto and Associate choreographer MAI Jingwen. Music by TIAM Mi. Music and orchestral arrangement by ZHOU Chuhang, LUO Geng, ZHANG Qun, ZHANG Qiandan, and ZHANG Boning. New York City Ballet Orchestra with Conductor LIO Kuokman.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

“Mamma Mia!” is back on Broadway for a limited engagement run, playing at the Winter Garden Theatre where it originally premiered in 2001. This limited run is scheduled to conclude on February 1, 2026, before hitting the road.

Besides feel-good, fun, and fabulous, I have three things to say about this show.

One, this show is part of the new, less-risky business model where a production first tests other cities, makes a short stop on Broadway (about six months), and then uses that momentum to head back on the road. Some similar shows that have done that recently are: The Wiz, Beetlejuice, and Annie. For producers, it means a show doesn’t have to sink or swim on Broadway before moving on, and for performers, it brings with it everyone who has been touring, granting many actors their well-deserved Broadway debut. The downside to this is that scenery has more limitations placed on it, as everything has to fit on a truck and is not designed specifically for the theater it is performing in. This is only a small quibble with my bar as to what a Broadway show is, as I do understand the practicality of it, and the Greek taverna location, consisting of two revolving set pieces, is imaginatively utilized in this production.

Two, Mama Mia! has been running somewhere in the world since its debut in 1999. Talk about longevity. It’s the ninth longest-running Broadway show with just shy of 6,000 performances (fifth longest-running, and still running since its debut in London). This has given it generational familiarity, which only leads to an anticipatory audience attending to spend time with an old friend. (Though that does not preclude those who don’t have that familiarity. The date I was with did not have a history with the show, was familiar with a couple of ABBA songs, and found herself dancing in the aisles and leaving the theater with a grin on her face as wide as Broadway.)

Just in case you don’t know, Mamma Mia! is the story of Sophie on the eve of her wedding. She has invited three men from her single mother’s diary (unbeknownst to mom) to the Greek island where she and her mom live to determine which one of them is her father. Thinking this will resolve all the questions she has about who she really is, she instead learns who she isn’t. The music in the show utilizes the songs of ABBA to creatively tell the story.

Three, this is a totally feel-good experience as the audience is already primed before the overture even begins. Vacation clothes, leis, and other show-themed garments are worn by a number of those attending, adding to the festive air of the theater. There is clapping and spontaneous sing-along to many of the show’s musical numbers that is welcomed by the performers. The actors are having as much fun as the audience, and that combination creates a sense of celebration that infects everyone there.

This two-and-a-half-hour respite from the world is what we all need right now.

—–

Mamma Mia!  features music and lyrics by ABBA’s Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus, a book by Catherine Johnson, direction by Phyllida Lloyd, and choreography by Anthony van Laast.

This current cast of Mamma Mia! is Christine Sherrill as Donna, Amy Weaver as Sophie, Carly Sakolove as Rosie, Jalynn Steele as Tanya, Rob Marnell as Harry Bright, Jim Newman as Bill Austin, Victor Wallace as Sam Carmichael, and Grant Reynolds as Sky.

Tickets are available right here

Running time: 2 hr 30 min (including intermission)

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

“Twelfth Night” is at the Delacorte.

Let me repeat that:

“TWELFTH NIGHT” IS AT THE DELACORTE!!

Bravo to the return of theatre to this glorious location!!!  Bravo to the hundreds of people who made it happen.  There is nothing like sitting under a fading sky, watching the birds zoom from tree to tree as well as the occasional raccoon – this one arrived early and tottled across the top of the back wall before slipping down the other side and off into the night..

Delacorte Raccoon; Photo Courtesy of David Laundra

You should know from the get go that I am not a Shakespeare aficionado.  For that you should look somewhere else.  I can, however, give you the nuts and bolts of this comedy. BTB – If it is a happy ending – with Shakespeare we call it a comedy.

Remember this was written over 300 years ago.  Run THAT up the flagpole.

Near the land of Ilyria (third star to the right as Peter Pan might have put it) a brother and sister are shipwrecked. Viola and Sebastian (played by the real life sister and brother Lupita Nyong’o and Junior Nyong’o)

The tale is narrated with music by the astonishing talents of  Moses Sumney.  Guitar n hand, he is our guide for the evening.

The siblings are separated with both thinking the other has drowned.  Viola disguises herself as a man, Cesario. (PS women did this ALL THE TIME back in the day, and still do, because it is safer to travel solo as a man.)  Cesario enters the service of Duke Orsino (Khris Davis).  Kaboom! She falls in love with the Duke.  Orsino, however, believing that Cesario is who he says he is, sends him off to act as a sort of proxy and woo Olivia (Sandra Oh) – a countess who just to happens to live in the neighborhood.  Cesario does as asked and, wouldn’t  you know it, Olivia falls for Cesario.  Another Kaboom! There is nothing to be done by Cesario except to avoid her advances.

Into the mix come Olivia’s Uncle, Sir Toby Belch (John Ellison Conlee) and his friend Andrew Aguecheek (Jesse Tyler Ferguson) as well as Fabian (Kapil Talwakar) who attends the Duke and and Maria (Daphne Rubin-Vega) the Gentlewoman attending Olivia.  These folk lighten the load of unrequited love by taking nothing seriously.

Except for ONE thing, and that is Malvolio (Peter Dinklage) a steward in the house of Olivia.  They take his puffed up pretense very seriously.  So seriously that they devise a plot to make him think that his mistress, Olivia, is in love with him.

Olivia is not.

So you see there are a lot of characters aimed at cross-purposes all going off half cocked and running into one another.

And did I mention Sebastian did NOT die?  Remember this is a comedy.

It takes awhile for us to get to the part where everything sorts itself out.  And even though a substantial portion of the script has been removed, the production till feels a bit sluggish.  (This is the part where I wish I could tell you exactly what – but no luck).

The production clocks in at 100 or so minutes.but it feels longer than that

The pacing imbalance kind of sneaks up on us.  Overall, the goings on are unclear and adrift.

Peter Dinklage; Photo by Joan Marcus

What is very clear, however, is that Dinklage has no trouble with pacing.  As a matter of fact he more or less leads the pack.  He is crisp, clear, concise of movement and knows what he wants.  This Malvolio is living off the air exhaled by his mistress.  So certain is Dinklage that his every appearance makes us sit up and pay attention.

The rest of the company does not fair as well.  They are all excellent performers – I have seen most of them shine.  So why it is that they, as a group, seem uncertain of the directions in which they are moving?

Who knows.

This does not make for a bad production.  It is uneven.   That could change for the better over the next few weeks.  This is live theatre, folks.  Each night will have its unique personality.

So I say YES get over to the Delacorte.  This is a banquet of revelry – a New York Treasure that Joseph Papp envisioned.  It is a gift to New York.

Curtain Call Cast of Twelfth Night; Photo by Joan Marcus

PS it also has the best curtain call EVER.  So good it makes you wonder why these actors had to wait so long to celebrate their riches.  What would the tale have been had these been the garments of the tale?

TWELFTH NIGHT by William Shakespeare, Directed by Saheem Ali

This production of Free Shakespeare in the Park’s TWELFTH NIGHT will be the seventh time Shakespeare’s classic comedy has been produced at The Delacorte. Previous iterations were produced in 1969(directed by founder Joseph Papp), 1986, 1989, 2002, 2009, and an adaptation for Public Works in 2018.

Scenic Design MARUTI EVANS, Costume Design OANA BOTEZ, Lighting Design BRADLEY KING, Composer/Orchestrations/Music Director, Choreographer DARRELL GRAND MOULTRIE, Swahili Dialect Coach KARISHMA BHAGANI, Music Supervisor SASHA BARTOL, Voice & Text Coaches JULIE CONGRESS & ANDREW WADE  Hair, Wigs, and Make-up Design KRYSTAL BALLEZA, Prop Manager CLAIRE M. KAVANAH, Fight Director THOMAS SCHALL

WITH DarioAlvarez(Ensemble),b (Antonio), John Ellison Conlee (Sir Toby Belch), Khris Davis (Orsino), Peter Dinklage (Malvolio), Jesse Tyler Ferguson (Andrew Aguecheek), Jaina Rose Jallow (Ensemble), Ariyan Kassam (Curio/Ensemble), Valentino Musumeci (Ensemble), Junior Nyong’o (Sebastian), Lupita Nyong’o (Viola), Chinna Palmer (Ensemble), Sandra Oh (Olivia), Precious Omigie (Ensemble), Nathan M. Ramsey (Ensemble), Daphne Rubin-Vega (Maria), Jasmine Sharma (Ensemble), Moses Sumney (Feste), Kapil Talwakar (Ensemble), Joe Tapper (Sea Captain/Priest), Julian Tushabe (Ensemble), Adrian Villegas (Ensemble), Ada Westfall (Ensemble), and Mia Wurgaft (Ensemble).

TWELFTH NIGHT features scenic design by Maruti Evans, costume design by Oana Botez, lighting design by Bradley King, co-sound design by Kai Haradaand Palmer Hefferan,composition byMichael Thurber, hair, wig, and makeup design by Krystal Balleza, prop management by Claire M. Kavanah, fight direction by Tom Schall, choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. Karishma Bhaganiserves as the Swahili dialect coach. Delacorte Veteran Buzz Cohenserves as the Production StageManager and Jessie Mooreand Luisa Sánchez Colónserve as the stage managers.

FREE TICKET INFORMATION  Performances of TWELFTH NIGHT begin at The Delacorte Theater on Thursday, August 7 and will continue through Sunday, September 14, with an official press opening on Thursday, August 21. The performance schedule will be Tuesday through Sunday at 8:00 p.m. (There will be no performance onTuesday, September 2and Wednesday, September 3). Tickets to The Public Theater’s Free Shakespeare in the Park are distributed in a number of ways.

Free tickets may be acquired on the day of the performance in person at The Delacorte Theater, in person at a borough distribution site (complete schedule canbe found on The Public’s website), via an in-person lottery in the lobby of The Public Theater at 425 Lafayette Street, or through a digital lottery via the TodayTix mobile app.

All tickets are subject to availability. There will be two American Sign Language Interpreted performances on Sunday, August 23 and Tuesday, August 26, both at 8:00 p.m. There Open Captioned performance in Englishwill be on Friday, September 5. There Open Captioned performance in Spanishwill be on Saturday, September 6.For the first time this summer, Free Shakespeare in the Park will offer a Sensory Adaptedperformance on Sunday, September 7. The Audio Describedperformance will be on Friday, September 12. A limited number of tickets are also available via advance reservation by making a contribution in support of Free Shakespeare in the Park. To learn more, or to make a contribution, call212.967.7555, or visitpublictheater.org.The full performance calendar and complete distribution details can be found at publictheater.org.The Delacorte Theater in Central Park is accessible by entering at 81st Street and Central Park West or at 79th Street and Fifth Avenue.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Take a Banana for the Ride

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

There are some shows that are self-contained. They exist for a moment, the moment you are in the theater, and then fade away. They take up no more space than however long the performance was. This is not that. Take a Banana for the Ride was expansive. It took up space. It carried itself out of the theater, in the mouths, and in the hearts of many leaving the theater.

It also had moments where it simply did not land. It definitely danced, fast and loose, with jokes, and many landed on a disappointing note. First and foremost–this is a life story, and it’s quite sad. That’s important to know going in.

Over the course of the evening, Jeff Ross described and poked fun at, but ultimately shared how much he loved, the forces that made him who he is today. He walked us through his life, with several musical interludes: his New Jersey roots, his family’s catering business, his parents and their love story, his relationship with his grandfather, and more. 

A highlight of the show was the section on the two german shepherds he adopted. Everyone was cackling. I have to chuckle to myself, just sitting here and writing about it. He described their personalities, his reluctance to take them in, and his absolute adoration for them. He told a fantastic story about taking his older dog, Nana, to the dog park and another one about Nana’s capacity to protect him. 

Another highlight was his tribute to three friends he lost, comedy geniuses among them. It was heartwrenching. Honestly, much of the night was. The show dipped downwards more than I expected. But it dipped back up, as well. 

The set created the mood for the evening: a blue couch in the middle of the stage, majestic frames rising up in the background. Sitting on the couch, Ross told a story about his grandfather and a difficult night. It made Ross’ caregiving come to life—attaching those aspects of Ross’ life and personality to an object, infusing that object with meaning. Even when Ross walked away, the couch kept a firm grip on our attention. Throughout the evening, the frames behind him lit up with pictures, giving a visual backing to the stories he was telling—an art show. It made the frames, even when empty, an emblem of memory.

There was also a banana next to the couch. Why a banana? Well, that, and the title of the show, was based on a quote of his grandfather’s—”take a banana for the ride,” he would say, handing Ross a banana when Ross headed out the door. The banana was his grandfather’s way of being with him, even when he couldn’t. At the end of the show, Ross handed us bananas. 

As I was leaving the theater after the show, I overheard someone telling their friend that this was the best show they’ve seen in a while. Many audience members were emotional. Many of the audience members truly resonated with the show. It was sadder than I expected, and not everything landed, but it certainly had heart to it. 

 

The show was written by Jeff Ross. It was directed by Stephen Kessler with creative consultation by Jeff Calhoun, dramaturgy by Seth Barrish, and music direction by Asher Denburg.

Tickets for Take a Banana for the Ride here. Running through September 28th at the Nederlander Theatre.

excerpt.rendered: Over the course of the evening, Jeff Ross gave us a comedy show that wasn’t. It was funny. It was also the story of his life. It was him.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

In Road Kills, playwright  Sophie McIntosh has devised that most elusive of creations — a truly original story.  From the unique premise to unexpected plot twists, Road Kills looks at what has been squashed on the pavement, literally and figuratively,  and what follows in its wake.  Delving into her premise, McIntosh speaks in moments.  She builds outward by moving inward, allowing the narrative to unfold in halting increments.  Nothing in this play is easy and yet it flows with humor and quiet intensity  It’s an extraordinary work.  Within minutes I was all in.

Owen (D.B. Milliken) owns a road kill retrieval business – yes, it’s a thing – and Jaki (Mia Sinclair Jenness) has been assigned to work six weeks’ community service with him for drunk driving.  Owen takes his job seriously, imbuing it with a kind of spiritual gravitas.  For Jaki, of course, it’s just something she has to get through.  It doesn’t help that the task is also nauseating.  As they scrape remains off the roads of Wisconsin, Owen and Jaki struggle to understand each other.  It is hard enough for them to communicate.  She is young and cynical; he is young and naive.  Jaki is all edges while Owen is deceptively smooth, almost featureless.  And yet nothing could be further from the truth.  Jaki may lash out at the world, but not every flame has to burn bright to cause injury.

As Jaki and Owen, Mia Sinclair Jenness and D. B. Milliken paint in rich colors.  They possess a subtle chemistry that flexes with the push and pull of their contentious, humorous, perplexing  interactions.  Jeness plays the sardonic humor without overdoing it, and when she pivots to drama she gets to the heart of it seamlessly.  Milliken burns like ice.  His drama is on the inside, looking for a way out.  Retrieving animal remains is a lonely business, and you feel it in the episodic structure of the play.  Each scene is a different road kill, set up in voice over.   Parachuting in on Jaki and Owen on some isolated road next to a new unfortunate animal, is like picking up a book where we left off.

All of this plays out on Junran “Charlotte” Shi’s spare, perfect set.  Economy is essential in a small theater, but still there are ways and ways.  A strip of asphalt, a bit of grass, and a ‘deer crossing’ sign and we have what we need.  Under Paige Seber’s clear, intentional lighting, the space expands beyond the confines of the small theater.  Nina Goodheart  directs with a similar economy and intelligence, balancing the laugh-out-loud humor with the constant undercurrent of tension.  It feels ‘hands off’ but it isn’t.

Maybe that’s what’s so striking –it all feels ‘hands off,’ yet without any danger of spinning out of control.  This play covers same delicate territory – abuse, trauma and one hell of a plot twist, but none of it is gratuitous.  The road kill itself is handled tastefully.  This is a play about damage, but McIntosh has written with such precision and Goodheart has handled so skillfully, you feel the damage, but you do not feel damaged.  McIntosh, in one of her many impressive small moments, finds a redemption we can hold on to.

Road Kills, by Sophie McIntosh, directed by Nina Goodheart.

With Mia Sinclair Jenness, D.B. Milliken and Michael Lepore.

Scenic design by Junran “Charlotte” Shi, lighting design by Paige Seber, costume design by Saawan Tiwari and props design by Sean Frank.

Presented by The Good Apples Collective and ryan duncan-ayala at the Paradise Factory (64 East 4th St.) Main Theater.  For tickets go HERE or to roadkillsplay.com.  Runtime 85 minutes, no intermission.  NOTE:  Issues of abuse, alcoholism, suicide and sexual behavior (no nudity) are addressed.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
by Margret Echeverria

I came to see Sulfur Bottom written by  Rishi Varma and directed by Megumi Nakamura  at The Theater Center fearing a sermon about how we Earth inhabitants are destroying the future with our unconscious lifestyles.  But rather than coming away feeling guilty and possessing no ideas for corrective action, I can report that what I experienced was a living portrait of a family surviving existence on a choking planet while still reaching for joy, love, belonging and understanding of one another.  The consciousness of these characters moves through all states – the unitary, the dream state, the mystical and the indescribable.  All this through using broad strokes of time-travel, shape-shifting and symbols of transformation as illustrative vehicles.  Rather than pulled by our ears to hard conclusions, the audience is gently held in revelatory visions.

Any Broadway casting director should have Joyah Dominique (Melissa) on speed dial.  Dominique’s instrument is utterly fluid embodying Melissa’s heart, through surprise humor, endearing physicality and intelligence.  She struggles with loyalty to family keeping her stuck and a personal purpose, which would lead her far from home.  Kevin Richard Best (Sir Cavin), Melissa’s brother, is slicing up Dominique in the first scene as she is first presented in the role of a dead deer.  The deer has been killed by Kendyl Davis (Fran), Sir Cavin’s daughter, after it kicked Fran in the head.  The deer lies upon the living room floor in a crumbling house sporting 1980’s wallpaper designs.  I felt my brain rubbing its sides together like eager hands tackling a fun riddle.  Davis and Best are the father daughter dynamic in which dad doesn’t always know best but daughter defers to respectful obedience rather than enlightening the patriarch or choosing loving separation.  Best and Dominique, rival siblings, spar when she speaks her unfiltered mind grounding Sir Cavin from lofty ideals.  That is, until Copal (Aaron Dorelien in the production I saw), the mealy-mouthed seductive devil, convinces Sir Cavin to trade uncertain future for instant gratification and illusions of security.  Copal then fools Melissa into sealing the deal, which shuts her up almost forever.  Fran’s resentment slowly smolders becoming a raging fire that turns Melissa’s dreams into dust and sucks the air out of this family’s tiny bottle of hope.

Feylsola Soetan (Maeve), is the characterization of the next generation.  If the pedigree of the wallpaper was not enough, Maeve has rainbows in her sleeves, wears a headband and industrial uniform with flair while smiling through the pain of the betrayal of promises made to her by her

Maeve (Feyisola Soetan): Left & Winter (Eric Easter): Right. Photo by Austin Pogrob

elders, letting us know she is a millennial.  Maeve, the daughter of Winter (Eric Easter) struggles in a father-daughter configuration that mirrors her mother Fran’s with Sir Cavin.  Winter’s need to be validated ignores his practical incompetence (some might say, “weaponized”).  Maeve fearlessly returns to the old homestead to discover truths hidden in the soil as she taps into ghosts visiting from her deceased family line, which includes her mother, Fran.  And I’m delighted to see Melissa again.  These scenes are like a dream.  You know how when your  eighty-year-old aunt explains mysterious pieces of your family history and you aren’t quite sure what really happened and what she is making up?  That is what these revelations feel like which, by the way, take place around the actual sulfur bottom – a blue whale – personified by Sir Cavin who we thought was also dead.  It’s a trip, folks.

A lingering disappointment in this show was that the set designer, Daniel Prosky, seemed a bit unaware of how the design of the theatre space would mesh with his vision.  The carpet was practically a character unto itself, yet our perspective is sitting below the stage level missing several other objects and character placements as well.  Perhaps Nakamura could have been more creative with the staging if raking the set was out of the question due to budget.   Off-Broadway often welcomes creativity more so than the canned productions down the street.  We certainly do get it here in a tight ensemble of characters co-mingling through relationships and grief transcending space and time.  Your mind may be so stimulated that you’ll swear you can smell the sulfured air of the industrial complex in the theatre.  And you’ll be left knowing that our most important investment, as we face the inevitible entropy of the universe, is in our relationships with other people and the joy that they bring.

SULFUR BOTTOM by Rishi Varma, directed by Megumi Nakamura

WITH Kendyl Davis (Fran), Kevin Richard Best (Sir Cavin), Joyah Dominique (Melissa), Eric Easter (Winter), Feylsola Soetan (Maeve), Isaiah Joseph (Copal), Tatiana Graves-Kochuthara (Female Swing), Aaron Dorelien (Copal/Winter Swing)

Set by  Daniel Prosky, lighting by Sam Welser, costumes by Roger Teng, sound design by Sid Diamond, music by Jacob Brandt.

Wednesdays at 7:30 PM and Saturdays at 1 PM through October 11, The Jerry Orbach Theater, The Theater Center, 210 West 50th Street, New York, NY.  Run time 90 minutes.  No intermission.  Get tickets here.  Or call (212) 921-7862.

@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

By Sarah Downs

The Day I Accidentally Went to War, Bill Posely’s one man show currently running at the SoHo Playhouse, is an engaging piece of autobiographical theater.  It is a tale of resilience, intuition and determination.  Posely is a natural, speaking from the heart as he takes us on a remarkable emotional journey in 75 short minutes.

As he narrates his personal history, Posely moves breezily between humor and emotional intensity to illuminate the facets of a life experience that comprises everything from childhood trauma to standup comedy to military service (and more trauma).  His authenticity draws us in.  The contradictions of his reality – a sensitive boy growing up in a tumultuous household, unsure of what the future held for him, joining the National Guard at 17 and returning home from war deeply changed, are rich fodder for his storytelling.  In normal circumstances, the National Guard don’t go into battle, but the demands of the war in Iraq activated him.  Hence the “accident” of his going to war.  And, I guess, the accident of his return.

Throughout his performance, with photographs, a few props, a bullhorn and audience participation, Posely builds community with the audience, one pun at a time.  The journey of his life has granted him a perspective beyond his years, yet at the same time he has maintained his capacity for wonder.  Charming and quick witted, Poseley is yet a man full of surprises, turning on a dime from looking at his life to reliving it.  The moments of emotional intensity are positively gripping.

Joining the military was not originally on his radar (no pun intended) but that’s where his life took him.  Indeed his path has taken him on various unlikely twists and turns, packing more experience into a short time than most of us would in a lifetime.  Posely was a soldier, he was on the tv show Survivor, he does stand-up, he writes, including for the (fabulous) show “Shrinking,” he acts.  It’s incredible.  As he describes his childhood, basic training deployment and his post-war experience, he paints a unique picture, one that challenges our received notions of what a ‘typical’ soldier looks like.  He enjoins us not to fall into the trap of assuming macho muscles and tattoos are it.

Posely’s story resonates even with those who have not served, in giving us permission to look at our own challenges, seeking both the lessons and the humor that lie therein.  All I could think as he talked of his war experience was ‘thank God Dad had asthma and flat feet.’  Seriously.  Sharing his story also opens the door within us to introspection and compassion – for others and for ourselves.  It also creates space for veterans to recognize themselves.  And that is very much the point of this show – not just to relay a unique tale and share a disarming sense of humor, it is also to remind us, to plead with us, not to forget our soldiers.

This truth telling is essential.  The criminal abandonment of soldiers upon their return from battle is one of our country’s most egregious failures.  All you have to see is one Wounded Warrior Project ad and you can see the extremity of the neglect.  I think feeding, housing and medical care are not too much to ask, yes?  Instead of a $48 million vanity birthday party – oops I mean military parade — why not comprehensive funding for the VA?  Use that $48 million for good.  Just a thought.  I mean, if leaders will continue to choose violence over diplomacy, sending innocent men and women off to battle (as long as it’s not their kids) veterans are going to need our help.  And they will deserve it.

The Day I Accidentally Went to War, by Bill Posely, directed by Bente Engelstoft and produced by Kristen Boulé.

Playing at the SoHo Playhose (15 Vandam St.) through August 30th.  Tickets HERE or at www.sohoplayhouse.com.  Runtime: 75 minutes with no intermission.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Jamie Allan stars in and is Amaze(ing).

This is, first and foremost, a tremendous magic show presented by a magician’s magician that will leave you astounded, no matter how cynical you are. And, secondly, and just as entertaining and wondrous, is the story of the making of a magician and his journey to finding the magic in his life, and urging you to find the magic in yours.

Now playing at one of New World Stage‘s smaller spaces, this is a show for all ages that

What Mr. Allan delivers is the story of his life, how he discovered his interest in magic at a young age, and the things that kept happening to him to lead him further down that path. (Remarkable story about his mother dragging him with her on one of her antique shopping sprees with the promise to look for a top hat for him to use in his magic, only to stumble upon a shop that did not have top hats, only magic hats.)

The setup is an intricately designed stage (kudos to set designer Damien Stanton) that is the attic of his memories, beginning with the first magic set he was ever given. From there, we are taken on a magic carpet ride of a journey from apprentice to the world-renowned magician that he is today. During this ride on the memory train, we are gifted with a display of magic from the most intimate (with help from the audience) to large illusions that mystify the logic of how matter is supposed to move in the world (a motorcycle from nowhere). Through this storytelling and display of wonder, Mr. Allan creates a beautiful personal connection with the audience that makes the show seem performed for each audience member individually.

Touching on the ethereal, he shared a dream that one day we would all assemble in this very spot together and watch him do a magic show. That happened, giving the audience a feeling that they were all part of something bigger than themselves, and giving us the gift that life’s long adventure should be lived with a source of wonder.

Amaze is a source of wonder.

—–

Amaze was created by Jamie Allan and Tommy Bond. Directed by Jonathan Goodwin.

Cast: Harry DeCruz, Natalia Love, Natalie Gerene, Justin Gentry

Creatives: Co-creator Tommy Bond, Graphic Designer Clare Nordbruch, Illusion director Richard Young, Set Designer Damien Stanton, Sound Design Ryan Borshuk.

Now performing at New World Stages Stage 5, 340 W 50th St, New York, NY 10019

Tickets can be purchased HERE.
