content.rendered:
By Vahni Kurra

The thing about ta-da! is: you’ve never seen anything like it, and trying to describe it feels almost as impossible as the theatrical feat it took to make it. Imagine a show whose format is inspired by the content-saturated culture we occupy, which has us scrolling our Instagram feeds as we watch TV on our laptops while notifications ping on our smart watches. Imagine a gay millennial’s stand-up special about grief and coming out combined with theatrical magic. And imagine it punctuated with perfectly timed dick jokes.

This is just a taste of the gleeful and ruminative comedy in Josh Sharp’s ta-da!, a solo show currently running at Greenwich House Theater (or “Grin Itch How’s” as his slides say). Yes, slides. As Josh explains with jester-like cheekiness, the comedic show tears through 2,000 PowerPoint slides in 80 minutes (that’s 1 slide every 2.4 seconds for the mathematically minded).

Credit: Emilio Madrid

Even for a seasoned performer like Sharp (his credits include Dicks: The Musical and F*CKING IDENTICAL TWINS), it’s a daunting task to memorize 2,000 cues, which must line up perfectly with each beat of his act. Sharp knows it, and he acknowledges that it’s a pretty masochistic thing to do for the sake of theatre. There is a reason for the madness, which becomes clear as Sharp rockets through the slides in increasingly more inventive ways for hilarious payoffs. He uses a Venn diagram to talk about the time he was “minorly gay bashed” by a drunk woman on the subway, shows us a viral video of his southern father screaming the words to Adele’s “Rolling in the Deep,” and leads the audience in chanting a strangely provocative yet satisfying phrase that a stranger in Florida once said to him (it’s better if you hear it from him).

The show is joyously provocative—not in the edgelord podcast host way, but in the way of your best friend telling you about their spiciest sexual escapades. Sharp wears a boyish grin as he describes steamy encounters in the Russian Turkish Baths (”gay men really do be getting hard anywheres”) and getting caught with porn as a teenager (”pubescent life is a waking Kafkaesque nightmare”). The show speaks directly to the cultural references and offbeat comedic sensibilities of its mostly gay, millennial audience, and the team working on the show reflects that style with Sam Pinkleton directing (fresh off his Tony win for Oh, Mary!). At the same time, Sharp has an empathetic softness that invites the audience into other perspectives, especially when it comes to talking about his upbringing in the South.

For all the deliciously dumb punchlines (”Tom K. Poop” comes to mind), Sharp’s most impressive talent is seamlessly weaving the humor into a deeper emotional tapestry. The second act turns into the story of how his mom “gently bullied” him into coming out of the closet when she was in remission from ovarian cancer, a disease which eventually killed her. He describes how she sought to genuinely “know and be known” by the people she loved, calling it her “Dali Mama Phase.” Sharp also delves into his near-death experience and the resulting concussion that caused a 40 minute blank space in his memory. “It felt like I’m living in the effect, without knowing the cause,” he tells us, shifting into a somber, yet still warm tone.

Sharp’s incisive musings on purpose and meaning in the face of death are truly moving, and his emphasis on the need to figure out how to best spend our time on this earth struck a cathartic note. It is clear that this has been the underlying foundation of the show all along. After all, what better way to remind us of our limited time than by sitting down for an 80 minute PowerPoint presentation where each slide disappears almost as soon as it appears? It is a magic trick that unfolds with the careful hand of a performer guided by true vision and purpose. There is the sense that Sharp has emerged from his near-death experience and the loss of his mother with a clarity that demands to be shared.

Josh Sharp’s ta-da! is an intimate reckoning with mortality, a coming-out memoir, and a parade of dirty jokes all strapped into one roller coaster of a show. It will make you remember to love being alive, not because every part of it is easy, but because we can make the time we have count.

—–

TA-DA! – Written and Performed by Josh Sharp

Directed by Sam Pinkleton, Produced by Mike Lavoie and Carlee Birglia

At Greenwich House Theater, 347-621-6024, greenwichhouse.org/theater/. Through August 23. Running time: 80 minutes. No intermission.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

 

David Dean Bottrell brought his newest one-man show, Teenage Wasteland: Thirteen, Fourteen, Fifteen, to the Dixon Place HOT festival, for one night only. The place was packed, to the rafters packed, teeming with anticipation to share the comedy, sadness, and joy of his fourth solo work.

At this point in his career, he knows how to handle a crowd, how to mold them, how to bring them in with pathos, and then flip to the funny, self-deprecating outtakes of his life. Teenage Wasteland is a celebration of the pluses and minuses of being alive and plummeting through the rollercoaster and funhouse of it all.

His three other shows, David Dean Bottrell Makes Love, Dear Mr. Bottrell, I Cannot Possibly Accept This, and The Death of Me Yet, have made a name for him as he’s traveled the country performing and passing out laughter and tears with each show, thus the sold-out show.

He was only too briefly back in New York with family (the Dixon Place audience) to use the catharsis of theater to purge himself, through us, so that we both can come out the other end cleansed. As he stated at the top of the show, if you’ve had a wonderful upbringing, a childhood with no worry or hardships, you should leave now, as this show wasn’t for you.

Everyone laughed, no one left, and everybody stayed. That unanimous response to his invitation to exit only reflected that life isn’t easy for anyone, and we can all laugh and learn from each other’s foibles, mistakes, and determined perseverance, on how to get through it all.

Teenage Wasteland: Thirteen, Fourteen, Fifteen consists of five stories (of “heartbreak, hard-ons, and hair”) about how David grew up and the pressures from family, school, friends, and church. Feeling like an outsider in all four, he reveals how he tripped and stumbled along to eventually find a path to who he is, and knowing that his past travails only added to the person he is today. One of his most strikingly personal statements of the evening, “If there’s no road for you, climb on a bulldozer and make one!” reflected his life spirit that he shared on the Dixon Place stage.

—–

Dixon Place is running their HOT festival, now through August 1. “Since 1992, this trailblazing summer festival sizzles with artists presenting queer theater, dance, music, literature, comedy, and homoeroticism for the whole family! The longest-running annual LGBTQ festival in the world, HOT! has been a pioneer of queer arts and culture for 29 years.”

David has two more shows in August on his current tour, Wellfleet, MA, and Hyannis, MA. If interested, you can find info HERE.

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

JOY: A New True Musical is a story of unrelenting resilience, the power of a single mother with an idea, and the work of believing in yourself and your work when your support system is strained.

A box of ideas and creations from young Joy (Nora Mae Dixon) sits center stage as we take our seats and wait for the stage to be transformed into Adult Joy’s (Betsy Wolfe) kitchen where her iconic mop will come to life. During the performance, we are introduced to many of the settings prominent in the rise of Joy’s inventions: her generational home’s kitchen, the QVC showroom, the television screen, Joy’s manufacturer’s office, and the court room.

The musical brings not only the light to inventor and businesswoman Joy Mangano (Betsy Wolfe) but just how far a woman can go with a dream and perseverance. The Tony Award Nominated actor Betsy Wolfe is fresh from Broadway’s & Juliet; she does radiate the Joy that drives the production, but she also emits this strong self-confidence and encouragement of hope in our own endeavors. Joy’s story is inspirational for any age and gender; anyone that needs a reminder that you CAN defy the odds, whether you’re pursuing a personal goal, growth, supporting your family, or inventing the newest product that will just make a simple household chore easier—or all of these simultaneously.

Photo by Joan Marcus

Joy is a single mother living in a household with her divorced parents–Mother Toots (Jill Abramovitz) and Father Rudy (Adam Grupper )–daughter Christie (Honor Blue Savage) and ex-husband Tony (Brandon Espinoza). She loses her job with the TWA and decides to not return to a desk job. As a woman who put her dreams aside to provide for her family, she struggles with the balancing act of her daughter’s soccer games, a mortgage, and being a mom, while setting her own creative passions on the back burner. Constant conflict between Joy and her mother emerge as they argue about how to support a family. This feeling of Toots not supporting her dreams tugs at Joy’s emotions as I imagine the simultaneous regret, guilt, and innovation she must feel as her Miracle Mop invention takes a roller coaster ride to success. She is essentially bargaining with providing a stable life for her family. It’s not easy to sell a product when there’s already significantly cheaper ones on the market, but QVC takes a chance on Joy and her Miracle Mop. What mom wouldn’t buy a cleaning product created, recommended, and sold by another mother?

From the prototype of a reflective dog collar that Joy made as a child, to her Miracle Mop, Joy discovers that her mother did in fact remember and save all of her ideas. As Joy battles legal problems with her mop’s patent, she goes to court, but everyone prepares her for an insurmountable loss and a debt that could consume her. While her father’s much-younger girlfriend (Jaygee Macapugay) had been the one to supply the finances to kickstart the Miracle Mop, she can also be the one to help her lessen the burden of the financial loss and legal battle. Will Joy give in after coming so far? We see her family finally unite in support of Joy, the successful business icon she is, and in her future, as she follows her dreams. This Miracle Mop truly comes to fit its name–not just for people around the country cleaning their floors but for the unification of Joy’s family.

Photo by Joan Marcus

While the music helps to carry us from one time stamp to the next, from one obstacle to each overcoming, it wasn’t the music or lyrics that grabbed me, nor did I walk away from the show with a need to dive into the newly-released album. Though some actors (specifically Betsy Wolfe, Honor Blue Savage, Adam Grupper) and had superb numbers and performance in itself. I feel as though anyone would enjoy a musical number with men singing about QVC, and the audience did eat this production up. If you are or ever have been a QVC shopper, you’ll get a kick out of this show, even outside the context of Joy’s true story.

Photo by Joan Marcus

JOY: A New True Musical; book by Ken Davenport; directed by Lorin Latarro; music and lyrics by AnnMarie Milazzo; music supervision and arrangements by Andy Einhorn, choreography by Joshua Bergasse. Additional material by Amanda Yesnowitz.

CAST: Betsy Wolfe (Joy), Jill Abramovitz (Toots), Adam Grupper (Rudy), Jaygee Macapugay (Lorraine), Brandon Espinoza (Tony), Honor Blue Savage (Christie), Paul Whitty (Cowboy Eddie), Charl Brown (Dan), Gabriela Carrillo (Ronni), Nora Mae Dixon (Young Joy).

ENSEMBLE: Dana Costello, Ryan Duncan, Gaelen Gilliland, Sydni Moon, Manuel Santos, Brian Shepard, Allysa Shorte, Alan Wiggins, Briana Brooks, Lael Van Keuren, Jerome Vivona.

CREATIVE TEAM: Anna Louizos (Scenic Design), Tina McCartney (Costume Design), Yael Lubetzky (Lighting Designer), Daniel Lundberg (Sound Designer), Tony Award nominee David Bengali (Projection and Video Design), Liz Printz (Hair and Wig Design), Jillian Zack (Music Director), Gary Mickelson (Production Stage Manager), with ShowTown Theatricals serving as general manager.

JOY: A True New Musical will run until Sunday, August 17, 2025 at Laura Pels Theatre at the Harold and Miriam Steinberg Center for Theatre (111 West 46th Street). Run time is 2 hours and 15 minutes, including one 15-inute intermission. Tickets can be purchased here or by calling (212) 719-1300.

Joy’s story is inspirational for any age and gender; anyone that needs a reminder that you CAN defy the odds, whether you’re pursuing a personal goal, growth, supporting your family, or inventing the newest product that will just make a simple household chore easier—or all of these simultaneously.

title.rendered: Shakespeare’s Mischief, Music, and Magic Beneath the City Lights

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

If you believe that Shakespeare belongs sequestered within marble theatres or ivy-wrapped institutions, think again. The Drilling Company’s 30th Anniversary season of Shakespeare in the Parking Lot presented an ebullient A Midsummer Night’s Dream, transforming a Lower East Side lot into a crucible of dreams, deception, and delight. The evening’s performance was nothing short of a gift to the city—one that held the audience spellbound until the final bows. When next this troupe emerges, make haste to witness how they spin gold from grit, dream from concrete, and Puckish mischief from traffic and tenements.

Marie Claire and Thammie Laine Quách. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Shakespeare for All—Freely Given and Gloriously Realized

In a civic gesture as magnanimous as it is rare, the second night of the company’s 30th anniversary was offered free to the public. Such accessibility is not a hollow token, but a sincere commitment to democratizing the sublime pleasures of Shakespearean theatre—proof that genius, when freely given, thrives in unexpected corners.

Left: Aria Marinelli (Cobwebb), Thammie Laine Quách (Mustardseed), Jasmin Gonzalez (Moth). Right: Dave Marantz (Oberon). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

The Concrete Jungle as a Faerie Wood

To behold A Midsummer Night’s Dream amid the Lower East Side’s urban tapestry was to encounter the city as you’ve never seen it. Street horns, the wail of sirens, the occasional sputtering of power tools, and a streetlamp that blinked uncertainly before settling into nocturnal duty all became unwitting members of the ensemble. Passersby paused, curious and captivated, their faces lit by both stage lights and starlight.

Layered into this ambient symphony were musical delights. Thammie Laine Quách, who also portrayed Mustardseed, sang and played guitar with a gentle, lyrical touch, infusing scenes with emotional depth and buoyant color. Complementing this was Marion Stenfort’s Snout, her unmistakably French accent bringing continental charm to the Mechanicals. At the same time, her tasteful accordion artistry lent an old-world texture that transcended time and place.

The Bard’s Web of Love, Lunacy, and Lament

Under the deft direction of Hamilton Clancy, the production navigated Shakespeare’s intricate web of intersecting narratives with clarity and verve. The play within a play, the chaotic entanglements of young love, the quarrels of faerie royalty—all were distinct threads woven seamlessly into a tapestry that was as understandable as it was enchanting.

Modern costumes blended the mundane with the magical, conjuring an aesthetic that was both familiar and fantastical. Props were imaginatively purposed, each piece propelling the story without overshadowing the audience’s imagination.

 

Dave Marantz, Una Clancy, Alessandro Colla. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

A Cosmopolitan Cast of Distinction

The international roots of this diverse cast echoed New York’s cosmopolitan spirit. Andy Rowell’s Puck, with his mischievous English accent and kinetic presence, seemed to materialize and vanish like an actual sprite, even darting through scenes atop a CitiBike—a delightful collision of Elizabethan whimsy and urban immediacy. His performance was a standout, embodying the play’s mercurial magic.

Lia Bonfilio delivered a Helena of remarkable pathos and humor, her laments and longings perfectly calibrated between comic self-pity and genuine heartbreak. Alessandro Colla’s Nick Bottom was pure theatrical gold—his bravura, boundless confidence, and deliciously pompous delivery made every moment of his onstage presence an event. His transformation into a donkey-headed fool was matched by his commanding yet foolish bravado, eliciting laughter of catharsis and affection.

Lia Bonfilio as Helena. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Adding to the global palette, Basil Lvoff, a Russian émigré, brought a subtle, endearing presence as Snug. His performance added a gentle earnestness to the Mechanicals, making their every misstep endearing.

Rude Mechanicals (L-R): Basil Lvoff (Snug), Alessandro Colla (Nick Bottom), Evangeline Fontaine (Peter Quince), Chris Martel (Flute). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Miranda Reilly (Hermia), Patrick Hart (Lysander), and Kaleb Baker (Demetrius) rounded out the youthful quartet with performances that captured the emotional chaos and ardor of young love, their sincerity making the ancient text feel freshly minted.

Miranda Reilly as Hermia. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Kaleb Baker (Demetrius). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Patrick Hart as Lysander. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Music, Supernatural Mayhem, and the Marvel of Language

Musical performances punctuated the play, never ornamental but rather essential threads in the narrative’s fabric. These contributions heightened the dreamlike atmosphere, while Shakespeare’s language—rendered with crystal clarity—reminded us that his verse remains unmatched in its beauty and insight.

Andy Rowell (Puck), Dave Marantz (Oberon). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

The antics of Oberon and Puck, whose good intentions unravel into delightful disorder, invited reflections on the unseen forces guiding human hearts: jealousy, love, ambition, and desire—timeless engines of the human condition. As the plot resolved into harmony, the production reaffirmed that though love may bewilder, all’s well that ends well in the Bard’s whimsical cosmos.

The Mechanicals: Artisans of Unpolished Delight

The “mechanicals,” a band of well-meaning Athenian tradesmen turned amateur thespians, delivered some of the evening’s most uproarious comedy. Led by Peter Quince (Evangeline Fontaine), their rehearsals of Pyramus and Thisbe in the parking lot became a meta-theatrical nod to the very premise of Shakespeare in the Parking Lot: creating art with few resources but infinite heart.

L-R: Thammie Laine Quách (Mustardseed), Aria Marinelli (Cobwebb), Jasmin Gonzalez (Moth). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Bottom’s show-stealing antics were perfectly matched by his companions: Francis Flute, Tom Snout, Robin Starveling, and Basil Lvoff’s endearingly shy Snug. Their hapless efforts and mismatched roles not only parodied the lofty art of theatre-making but also celebrated it, echoing the Drilling Company’s mission. Indeed, their hilariously misguided play-within-the-play provided a charming counterpoint to the magical and romantic chaos surrounding them.

Evangeline Fontaine (Peter Quince), Chris Martel (Flute). Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Why This Production Resonates Now

In a city of perpetual flux and fleeting attention, this Midsummer Night’s Dream demonstrated the endurance of Shakespeare’s insights into human nature—its vanities, vulnerabilities, and victories. The combination of an international cast of artistic excellence, eclectic music, mystical supernatural fantasy, and urban staging rendered the play immediately relevant: a testament that the bardic mirror still reflects us, with all our modern follies intact.

L-R: Lizabeth Allen, Una Clancy, Davie Marantz, Miranda Reilly. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

As Opening Night Online insightfully observes about the Drilling Company’s approach, “Shakespeare in the Parking Lot remains one of New York’s most radical and democratic theatrical experiences—30 years on, it’s still making magic with asphalt, headlights, and heart.”

Foreground: Andy Rowell as Philostrate. Photo by Jonathan Slaff

Cast

  • Theseus/Oberon: Dave Marantz
  • Hippolyta/Titania: Una Clancy
  • Changeling Boy: Marie Claire
  • Egea: Lizabeth Allen
  • Helena: Lia Bonfilio
  • Hermia: Miranda Reilly
  • Lysander: Patrick Hart
  • Demetrius: Kaleb Baker
  • Bottom: Alessandro Colla
  • Peter Quince: Evangeline Fontaine
  • Flute: Chris Martel
  • Snout: Marion Stenfort
  • Starveling: Adama Joy Sall
  • Snug: Basil Lvoff
  • Puck: Andy Rowell
  • Cobweb: Aria Martinelli
  • Mustardseed: Thammie Laine Quách
  • Moth: Jasmin Gonzalez

Artistic and Production

  • Director: Hamilton Clancy
  • Assistant Director: Kathleen Simmonds
  • Original Songs: Thammie Laine Quách and Marion Stenfort
  • Additional Music: Chris Martel
  • Graphics: Andy Rowell
  • Table Design: Stephen Tarito
  • Signage: Shaun Lee
  • Publicist, Theatrical Photographer, and Actor: Jonathan Slaff

This performance was presented at 145 Stanton Street, New York, NY, on the Lower East Side, with entrance on Suffolk Street.

Performances are free, and seats are available on a first-come, first-served basis. Audience members often arrive early to secure a place. Audience members are welcome to bring their own chairs. Once seats are gone, blankets are spread out. No one has ever been turned away, and there’s never a wait for tickets.

Shakespeare in the Parking Lot. Artwork by Andy Rowell, Stephen Taritol and Shaun Lee

To learn more about this remarkable troupe’s mission to bring free, accessible theatre to all New Yorkers, visit www.drillingcompany.org. Runtime 120 minutes without intermission.

excerpt.rendered: In this unassuming parking lot, under an indifferent city sky, The Drilling Company conjured faeries, fools, and lovers in riotous splendor. Don’t just dream of theatre—see it lived, loud and luminous.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Four Irishmen and a lass walk into a bar and tell some ghost stories. No joke—that, in short, is the premise of Conor McPherson’s atmospheric drama, The Weir. Set in a pub in 1998 rural Ireland and consisting primarily of monologues, the work does not so much have a beginning, middle, and end as it has a beginning and five middles. Irish Repertory Theatre director Ciarán O’Reilly calls on a veteran cast to make the play palatable, and they do not disappoint, together offering an engaging interpretation of a piece that, if structurally curious, at least features the three pillars of any good Irish play: loss, regret, and loneliness.

The opening scene is devoted to introducing the characters, who blow into the pub amid—metaphor alert—unusually strange winds. First through the door is Jack (Dan Butler), a bachelor in his fifties who runs the local garage when not playing the horses. Next comes Brendan (Johnny Hopkins), a quietly successful chap who owns both the pub and the farmland that surrounds it. Brendan, too, is unmarried, as is Jim (John Keating), who works for Jack. He is saddled with caring for his mother. As Brendan explains, “She’s been very sick…for years now. Fading fast, like, for years!”

It is clear that the men get together regularly to gossip and hoist drinks. Many, many drinks. Their limited world is reflected in the pub’s meager offerings. It’s either Guinness or Harp, though the latter is not for the likes of a working man. And if it’s not stout, then it’s “a small one,” a.k.a. a shot of Jameson, though naturally nobody has just one. This evening’s gossip centers around Finbar (Sean Gormley), a wealthy, married businessman who has been seen with Valerie (Sarah Street), a younger woman who is not his wife.

When the two stop in at the pub, it becomes obvious that their relationship is far from salacious. Valerie is newly arrived from Dublin and moving into a house down the road. Finbar, who has just been showing her around, tellingly orders a Harp. Valerie requests wine, which sends Brendan scurrying, and soon enough the men’s banter turns to storytelling. First it is Jack, who relates the tale of Maua Nealon, whose house was built on a fairy road. The most terrifying part of the anecdote is offered as a minor detail barely worth a mention, involving a “fierce load of dead birds all in the hedge.”

Finbar weighs in with an account of a former neighbor who sees a ghost on the stairway, an event that, at the time, shocked Finbar out of his lonely life. Then Jim outdoes him with a story of when he was once hired as a gravedigger, only to be visited by the apparition of a man with a horrifying request as to where he wanted to be interred.

Not to be left out, Valerie chimes in with a personal, devastating narrative that echoes elements of the men’s: “There was someone coming up the stairs. There were children knocking, in the wall. And there was always a man standing across the road.” With the night reaching its end, Jack relates one more story—not a ghost tale per se, but one filled with his regret over a woman who could have been his wife. In the most haunting of confessions, he laments, “There’s not one morning I don’t wake up with her name in the room.”

As Jim, Keating (in his twenty-eighth production with the Irish Rep) gives his usual assured performance. Street, who was brilliant in the Rep’s recent Beckett Briefs, has less to do here but delivers admirably. Hopkins is quite fine as Brendan, a supporting character tasked more with listening than telling. And Butler and Gormley shine in their passive-aggressive friendship, two sides of the same coin. To say that the actors are well practiced is to note that O’Reilly directed Keating, Butler and Gormley in these same roles in the Rep’s 2013 revival. Meanwhile, scenic designer Charlie Corcoran’s realistic pub is both welcoming and thirst-inducing, making even the Harp look delicious.

 

The Weir – By Conor McPherson, directed by Ciarán O’Reilly

WITH: Dan Butler (Jack), Johnny Hopkins (Brendan), John Keating (Jim), Sean Gormley (Finbar) and Sarah Street (Valerie).

Set design by Charlie Corcoran, lighting design by Michael Gottlieb, costume design by Leon Dobkowski, sound design by Drew Levy and properties by Deirdre Brennan. The  Irish Repertory Theatre, 132 West 22nd St., 212.727.2737, https://irishrep.org.  Through August 31. Running time: 100 minutes

Photo: Sarah Street, John Keating, Dan Butler, Johnny Hopkins, and Sean Gormley. ©Carol Rosegg.

title.rendered: A Night of Chamber Music Excellence at the 92nd Street Y

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

The summer air buzzed with anticipation at the 92nd Street Y on July 9, 2025—an evening that, quite frankly, achieved the nonpareil of chamber music. The famed trio—Joshua Bell (violin), Steven Isserlis (cello), and Jeremy Denk (piano)—offered a program of Gabriel Fauré that was more than a performance; it was poetic communion.

Violinist Joshua Bell and Pianist Jeremy Denk on stage at the 92nd Street Y. Photo by Michael Priest Photography

Before the full trio convened, Bell and Denk took the stage alone, setting a sublime tone for the evening. From the first notes of Fauré’s Violin Sonata No. 1, Bell’s artistry and blinding radiance commanded rapt attention. His violin sang with a graceful, glittering, and luminous beauty that seemed to transcend the instrument itself, every phrase shaped with musical intelligence and lyric rapture. Denk’s accompaniment wasn’t merely supportive—it ineffably unfolded into a full-bodied, articulate partnership, revealing the sophisticated harmonic afflatus, emotional treats, and irresistible magnetism of Fauré‘s oeuvre.

Steven Isserlis, Cellist. Courtesy stevenisserlis.com

Fauré’s Violin Sonata No. 1: A Sublime Opening Duo

The Andante unfolded with dark, pensive expressiveness and lofty grandeur. Bell drew out lush subtleties as if coaxing a confession from the air. The Scherzo erupted with brightness—virtuosic, electric, playful. In the Finale, Bell’s bravura fused with lyricism and flair, delivering lilting melodies of exquisite lightness. Together, Bell and Denk set a standard of emotional and technical vigor.

L-R Steven Isserlis, Joshua Bell, Irene Duval, Blythe Teh Engstroem, and Jeremy Denk on stage at the 92nd Street Y. Photo by Michael Priest Photography

The Trio Unites: Barcarolle No. 5

When Isserlis joined Bell and Denk, the ensemble transitioned to Barcarolle No. 5, which emerged as a dramatic cantilena of pure virtuosity. The violin offered lyrical verses, the piano painted harmonic color, and the cello lent depth—a poetic trialogue shaded in chiaroscuro sonic textures. As this trio began, those of us present couldn’t help but summon the spirit of the Million Dollar Trio—Heifetz, Rubinstein, Piatigorsky—so seamless and magnetic was tonight’s magic.

Jeremy Denk, Pianist. Courtesy jeremydenk.com

Piano Trio in D Minor, Op. 120: Chamber Intimacy

Fauré’s Piano Trio in D Minor, Op. 120 followed, enveloping the audience in gentle musical orisons and majestic utterances. Denk’s piano waltzed through Fauré’s inspired chromaticism; Isserlis’s cello offered orotund, meditative lines; Bell’s violin soared with tender clarity. Their ensemble work formed a tapestry of intimacy that was sublime, subtle, and a profoundly human product of a well-crafted mélange.

Joshua Bell, Jeremy Denk, and Steven Isserlis on stage at the 92nd Street Y. Photo by Michael Priest Photography

Isserlis Shines in Solo Moments

After intermission, Isserlis returned for two beloved Fauré solo works: Sicilienne, Op. 78 and Berceuse, Op. 16. He delivered a delectation of heartfelt lyricism and crystalline tone. Each phrase felt newly minted, expressive, warm, and trance-inducing. “Heartwarming,” someone whispered nearby. Indeed, these assiduous moments of painted tones felt like quiet gifts.

Irène Duval, Violinist. Courtesy ireneduval.com

Piano Quintet No. 1 in D Minor, Op. 89: The Evening’s Pinnacle

The program culminated with Piano Quintet No. 1, featuring marvelous guest artists Iréne Duval (violin) and Blythe Teh Engstroem (viola). This performance was the apotheosis of the night. Every gesture and breath radiated power, ebullience, freshness, and a complex effervescence. The picturesque interplay between strings and piano reached a near-telepathic level. Fauré’s genius—his rich coloration, narrative arcs, harmonic depth, and Rossinian joie de vivre—was vividly realized through fluency, finish, and virtuosity.

As the final ravishing chords faded after soaring dramatic heights of artistic depth, confidence, brilliance, and power, the hall held its breath. Then, applause thundered. It was not merely approbation; it was recognition that we had experienced an evening at the summit of art—a communal acknowledgement of something extraordinary.

Blythe Teh Engstroem, Violist. Courtesy sion-violon-musique.ch

Why This Performance Mattered

This was no ordinary program. Each work showcased a different chapter in Fauré’s artistic evolution—from youthful passion to refined emotional clarity. The Violin Sonata, still performed in conservatories worldwide, bridges the gap between Romanticism and modernism. The Barcarolle and Trio Op. 120 explore lyrical refinement and introspective charm. The Piano Quintet remains a pinnacle of late Romantic nuance, bringing the genre to its apogee.

Even more compelling was the human element: Bell catching Isserlis’s eye, Denk exchanging a silent smile—glimpses of genuine camaraderie and shared joy. These weren’t just performances; they were personal revelations. As Leonard Bernstein once said, “Music can name the unnameable and communicate the unknowable.” On this night, that axiom describing the most ephemeral of the arts rang true.

Portrait de Gabriel Fauré (1845-1924), compositeur. P2651. Farré, Henry (Foix, 13–07–1871 – Chicago, en 07–10–1934), peintre, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Musicians as Storytellers

The evening offered insights gleaned from OpeningNight’s essays on symphonic storytelling and explorations of emotional architecture in performance. This concert provided living proof of music’s capacity to both transport and transform.

A Concert to Remember

This was a concert where every phrase felt freshly minted, yet deeply rooted. The 92nd Street Y’s intimate setting served as the perfect chamber for world-class artistry—artistry that reminded us why we gather to hear music live. It connected intellect and spirit, technique and heart, tradition, and spontaneity. Like those who recall the Million Dollar Trio, tonight we witnessed a piece of music history.

Even for those new to Fauré, the concert served as a welcoming gateway into his exquisite, luminous world. It left one hungry for more—more chamber music, more moments like these, more living artistry.

Million Dollar Trio. L-R: 1. Portrait of Jascha Heifitz. Rijksmuseum, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons. 2. Arthur Rubinstein Performing in Concertgebouw, Bestanddeelnr (1962). Wim van Rossem for Anefo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons. 3. Portrait of cellist Gregor Piatigorsky, in concert at Strasbourg (1930). Bibliothèque nationale de France, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Don’t Miss What Comes Next

The next performance in the Midsummer MusicFest series takes place on July 12. If you cherish musical elegance and expressive depth, this is your summer sanctuary. For anyone seeking the transcendence of live chamber music, the 92nd Street Y is the place to be. Be sure to check out the summer 2025 and 2025-26 season.

Bell, Isserlis, Denk, Duval, and Engstroem delivered a night of music-making that will linger in memory—a night where Fauré’s introspective muse met performers of eloquence, vitality, and soul. And together, they made magic.

The 92nd Street Y, New York

1395 Lexington Avenue
(between 91st & 92nd streets)
New York, NY 10128
For tickets and information, click HERE.

By Edward Kliszus

The Gene Frankel Theatre is where fact surrenders to legend and ideals confront the barrel of a gun.

Jethro Compton’s stage adaptation of The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance returns with a vengeance not of blood, but of conscience. Based on Dorothy M. Johnson’s short story that inspired John Ford’s 1962 cinematic parable starring James Stewart and John Wayne, this production, directed with muscular delicacy by Thomas R. Gordon, unveils itself as a finely tuned meditation on moral architecture: its fragility, its failures, and its strange triumphs.

The Sound of a Nation’s Conscience: Johnny Cash and the Sonic Landscape

Before a single line is uttered or a pistol drawn, the production establishes its spiritual geography through sound. Audience members are welcomed into the twilight of the American frontier by the unmistakable timbre of Johnny Cash’s voice—resonant, weathered, and unrelentingly sincere. These recordings, judiciously placed at the top of the show and during scene transitions, do not function merely as atmospheric adornments. Instead, they serve as emotional footnotes to the unfolding narrative. From themes of redemption and regret to justice and vengeance, Cash’s music—soaked in gospel, grit, and gravel—amplifies the play’s more profound philosophical musings. His songs do not interrupt the drama; they prefigure and echo it, as though the man in black himself was strumming chords beneath the floorboards of Twotrees. In this way, the production’s sparse but potent use of music roots the audience not just in time and place, but in mood and meaning.

The Western Reborn: Not Gunsmoke, but the Smoke of Ethical Reckoning

Let us dismiss, at the outset, any notion that this is a “Western” in the customary sense. If one seeks spectacle, one will be disappointed. If one seeks truth—elusive, wounded, profound—one will be rewarded. Here, the vast frontier is not a place of unspoiled freedom but a crucible where idealism is tempered by blood and silence.

Leighton Samuels and Mari Blake in a scene from The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance at the Gene Frankel Theatre. Photo by Joshua Eichenbaum.

The play opens with an unconscious stranger dragged into a saloon. This, one might think, is mere melodrama. But what unfolds is something far more penetrating. Ransome Foster (played with finely wrought gravitas by Leighton Samuels) is no brawling frontiersman. He is an intellectual émigré from the East—a man whose weapons are grammar and morality. And yet it is this gentle man who, by legend or necessity, becomes the titular executioner of Liberty Valance.

Performances of Principle: Actors as Moral Instruments

Samuels, in the role of Foster, delivers not just a character but an evolution—his arc a study in reluctant transformation, from cerebral scholar to mythic symbol. His interactions with Hallie Jackson (Mari Blake) do not merely enact romance, but the philosophical courtship between hope and complex reality. Blake is simply magnificent, portraying a woman whose very survival hinges upon the preservation of dignity amidst dust and danger.

And then there is Derek Jack Chariton’s Liberty Valance—a study in pathology. This is not villainy for the sake of villainy, but rather the embodiment of amorality weaponized by fear. Chariton’s Valance is not loud but low, not erratic but eerily focused. One senses, in his performance, the quiet horror of those who destroy not from wrath but from the void.

Samuel Shurtleff’s Bert Barricune, meanwhile, radiates quiet pathos. His love for Hallie, unconsummated and perhaps unrequited, is a tragedy unto itself—a man fighting not for the woman, but for the time when he might have won her. In his eyes, the audience sees a life postponed too long.

Leighton Samuels as Ransome Foster and Samuel Shurtleff as Bert Barricune in The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance at the Gene Frankel Theatre. Photo by Joshua Eichenbaum.

Production Design as Ethical Environment

To speak of the stagecraft is to acknowledge how character extends beyond flesh. Nino Amari’s set does not merely suggest a saloon—it is the saloon, imbued with the scent of pine, sweat, and whiskey. Susan Yanofsky’s costuming is neither ostentatious nor self-conscious; instead, it inhabits the actors as naturally as their dialects. Reid Sullivan’s lighting, too, plays its part in this moral chiaroscuro, where truth and myth flit like shadows in a lamplit room.

And how rare, how welcome, the restraint in sound design. The gunshots are few, and precisely for that reason, they resonate. They do not startle; they conclude. They do not thrill; they judge.

A Play of Moral Dimensions: Race, Power, and the Responsibility of Narrative

As Jim “The Reverend” Mosten, Daniel Kornegay is a quiet revelation with a tender heart and spirit. But his portrayal does not plead for sympathy; it commands respect. In a land where literacy is revolution, Mosten represents the deepest threat to tyranny—hope rooted in knowledge. His fate is a moral fulcrum upon which the entire narrative pivots, and Kornegay’s performance imbues the tragedy with dignity and devastating restraint.

There is a subtextual richness in this revival that speaks powerfully to contemporary audiences. The script’s measured pacing—often verging on elongation—might, in lesser hands, seem indulgent. But here, these moments act as crucibles of anticipation, akin to the loaded silence before a verdict or the breath before a shot.

Leighton Samuels and Daniel Kornegay in a scene from The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance at the Gene Frankel Theatre. Photo by Joshua Eichenbaum..

The Myth of the Gunman—and the Gunman of Myth

In its denouement, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance resists the cheap catharsis of victory. There is no triumph here, only a sacrifice at the altar of public need. Ransome Foster does not emerge as a man reborn, but as a fabrication—an emblem, a myth carved from necessity rather than truth. It is, as George Bernard Shaw might sharply observe, the most lamentable of all metamorphoses: the surrender of the individual’s truth to the collective’s appetite for illusion.

For Shaw, such a transformation would not be tragic because it is a lie, but because it is a useful lie—a fiction palatable enough to be mistaken for virtue. In his worldview, utility masquerading as morality is the grimmest comedy of all. That Foster is celebrated not for his integrity but for the myth others require of him is no triumph of character, but a capitulation to the herd’s preference for legend over reality.

And herein lies the most subversive question of the play: Is the fiction that consoles more righteous than the truth that convicts? And if we are to “print the legend,” as the old newspaperman suggests, who becomes the real casualty—those who believe it, or those erased by it?

Derek Jack Chariton plays Liberty Valance in The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance at the Gene Frankel Theatre. Photo by Joshua Eichenbaum

Summoning the Myth, Challenging the Truth: Come See Liberty Valance Live

Thomas R. Gordon directs with an intact moral compass. He neither glorifies nor vilifies, but allows each character—and each silence—to speak its whole truth. What results is not a play about the Old West, but about the old question: what is justice, and who gets to define it?

Thus, we experience a gripping, gorgeously acted parable of power, truth, and sacrifice.

This western isn’t about bullets—it’s about belief. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance is vital, eloquent theatre. Do not miss it.

Samuel Shurtlef and Daniel Kornegay in a scene from The May Who Shot Liberty Valance at the Gene Frankel Theatre. Photo by Joshua Eichenbaum

The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance

The Onomatopoeia Theatre Company

The Gene Frankel Theatre, 24 Bond Street (Between Lafayette & Bowery)
Wed-Sat at 8; Sat & Sun at 2
Through July 26, 2025
For tickets  and information ($25-$35), visit Onomatopoeia

Runtime is about 120 minutes with an intermission.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Dark times demand a dark musical and with its sociopathic leading man, a body count of snuffed out high schoolers, plus the lure of suicide as a leitmotif.  Heathers: The Musical certainly delivers the heebie-jeebies. But, like an anxious teen from a broken home, the jam-packed staging tries extra hard to please. The book and score by Kevin Murphy and Laurence O’Keefe want to be earnest as much as they want to be twisted, wish to be empowering as much as they wish to be bleak. The result, under the breakneck direction of Andy Fickman, is that there is something for everyone, but little that feels sincere. Thankfully, a powerhouse sextet of women are on hand, blissfully belting their way through the madness, in a captivating show of strength.

First and foremost there is Lorna Courtney in the lead role of Veronica Sawyer. Courtney, Tony-nominated for her work in & Juliet, sings like an angel though her character here has no shortage of inner demons. Wishing to avoid being bullied at school, she endears herself to the three Heathers (McKenzie Kurtz, Elizabeth Teeter, and Kiara Lee in for Olivia Hardy on the night I attended). Each is an evil treat that comes candy-color coated for easy digestion. Costumed and lit in flaming red, Heather Chandler is the boss of the other two and Kurtz has a great time in the role, showing off her fine voice and sharp comic timing while dressing down her curious yellow and envious green cohorts.

This above-it-all trio, at the top of their school’s food chain, are not beyond creating acts of cruelty for their own amusement, and Veronica plays along. Soon she is fully one of their gang, dressed in blue so as not to encroach, and embracing her new found external beauty while not taking heed of her better judgment. “It’s more like the Heathers are people I work with and our job is being popular and shit,” she observes.

Veronica’s life becomes even more complicated when she falls hard for the disturbingly quiet bad boy, J.D. (Casey Likes). Choosing his attentions over those of the Heathers is a slippery slope that soon turns murderous as she assumes a willful ignorance while J.D. dispatches the most powerful of the Heathers, then follows up by eliminating Ram and Kurt (Xavier McKinnon, Cade Ostermeyer), two bullying jocks who were spreading lies about Victoria. Staging the murders to look like suicides leads a number of their fellow students to consider harming themselves, none more devastatingly so than Victoria’s childhood pal, the unpopular Martha Dunnstock (Erin Morton), who sings a heart-rending goodbye to childhood and to life, “We will fly through the dawn/to a new kindergarten/where nap-time is centuries long.”

The sixth of the mighty female voices belongs to Broadway veteran Kerry Butler as the hippie teacher, Ms. Fleming. It is a relatively minor role but Butler blows the roof off the New World Stages theater with her one big number, “Shine A Light.”

In Heathers, the film, J.D. was portrayed by a young Christian Slater and it was easy to understand how he proved irresistible to Veronica. Casey Likes has a harder time of it. His Broadway credits include the nice guy roles in Back to the Future and Almost Famous. Playing against type here, he seems more mechanical than ominous and fails to conjure any chemistry with Courtney, despite his character’s mastery of explosives. 

Too bad Likes didn’t inherit the creepiness Ben Davis brings to the role of J.D.’s father, Bud. He is one of four dads in the play, all of whom are displayed as terrible parents. Veronica’s father (Cameron Loyal) is totally withdrawn while Ram’s and Kurt’s dads (also Davis and Loyal) are first shown as the reason their kids became bullies, then are quite improbably drawn to each other after the deaths of their sons. Then again, if even the brutish fathers of jocks can find their sensitive sides, there just might be hope for the “freaks” and “losers,” and their tormentors, who manage to survive the crucible of high school.

 

Heathers The Musical – Book, music and lyrics by Kevin Murphy and Laurence O’Keefe, directed by Andy Fickman.

WITH:  Lorna Courtney (Veronica Sawyer), Casey Likes (JD), McKenzie Kurtz (Heather Chandler), Olivia Hardy (Heather Duke), Elizabeth Teeter (Heather McNamara),  Kerry Butler (Ms. Fleming/Veronica’s Mom), Erin Morton (Martha Dunnstock), Xavier McKinnon (Ram Sweeney) Cade Ostermeyer (Kurt Kelly), Ben Davis (Ram’s Dad/Big Bud Dean/Coah Ripper), Cameron Loyal (Kurt’s Dad/Veronica’s Dad/Principal Gowan), Sara Al-Bazali, Emma Benson, James Caleb Grice, Louis Griffin, Devin Lewis, Kiara Michelle Lee, Brian Martin, Lav Raman, Syd Sider, and Cecilia Trippiedi. 

Choreography by Gary Lloyd, additional Choreography by Stephanie Klemons, Set and Costume Design by David Shields, Lighting Design by Ben Cracknell, and Sound Design by Dan Samson. New World Stages, (340 W. 50th St.), https://newyork.heathersthemusical.com/. Through January 25, 2026. Running time: 2 hours 30 minutes

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

Out of Order is Carl Holder’s autobiographical “Russian Roulette.” The show, acted out and written by Carl Holder, physically, logistically, and emotionally centers around a jar in the center of the room. Inside the jar is a plethora of pre-written notes–a mixture of moments from his life and fable-like messages. He reaches in and takes the notes out at random. One after the other after the next. So, while the show is scripted, the order of events is not.

It’s a fascinating concept, but the implementation is weak.

The show does well with questions. One of my favorite moments centers around Carl next to a lamp, switching from age to age to age, demonstrated aptly by posture and voice, muttering the same question: “How long do I have to wait?” The question does, indeed, take on vastly different meanings from age to age.

Indeed, flexibility is a strength of the show. Moments can serve different meanings and have different interpretations depending on where they happen to fall, happen to be plucked out of the jar. They are specific in and of themselves. But they’re flexible in where they show up. I did enjoy the war between flexibility and specificity throughout the show.

He does well with different characters and different impersonations, and that certainly is a strength of the show.

But the ding at the end of each scene, and the frantic run back to the jar and into the next scene, is deeply jarring. It adds a layer of false sincerity to the whole thing. A sense of panic. A rush that isn’t necessary. It undermines the truth of the matter and makes it feel like another run to…nowhere. This is exemplified by the coldness of the message at the end. There’s nowhere to run to, he seems to be claiming. So, I have to ask, why are we running?

And then, unfortunately, there’s the audience participation component. I’ve seen many shows with audience participation and they do a fabulous job–they get people to participate but they don’t make anyone do anything. They find the people in the room who want to. Never have I ever seen a show force people into participating in the way this show did.

At one point in the show, Carl forced us all to take pictures of him and demanded that we post it on social media. I take no issue with the request to post. What I take ABSOLUTE issue with is the way he walked around and stared down at our phones, watching as and until we posted. What I take even more issue with is the way he forced anyone who didn’t have social media or didn’t want to post to stand up and yell promotional phrases out the door. It was outrageous. I truly hope this changes during the course of the show’s run.

A lot of the show was honest in a good way. Another great moment was a scene with a trash can, with predictions of what could be on the table before age 40. And the idea of asking for help was strong. In both of those scenes, audience participation was done well. With some tweaks around audience participation in other scenes, this could be a show that everyone could enjoy.

The show is running at the East Village Basement until July 22nd. You can purchase tickets here.

WRITTEN & PERFORMED BY CARL HOLDER

DEVELOPED WITH & DIRECTED BY SKYLAR FOX

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

New York Theatre Company’s revival of Machinal at New York City Center Theatre 2 is an extraordinary, revelatory dissection of a play about patriarchy and repression, as relevant today as when it was written in 1928.  The performance has a plasticity that blurs the lines between theater and spontaneous expression, creating theatrical poetry that is not to be missed.  It is one heck of an Off-Broadway debut.  Director Amy Marie Seidel and choreographer Madison Hilligoss honor the original text, capturing and building on its Expressionist roots through the interpolation of stylized gesture, sound, dance and music.  In so doing they have taken a wordy, static play and transformed it into a multi-dimensional, multi-disciplinary production that is yet laser focused.

The play by Sophie Treadwell is based loosely on the story of Ruth Snyder, who was sent to the electric chair for murdering her husband.  Machinal explores the circumstances in which a woman could be driven to make such a choice.  Sadly, these circumstances affect us as much today as they did in 1928.  Helen (Katherine Winter) is a stenographer in a small office.  The other ‘girls’ are chatty, even raucous, teasing Helen for being their boss’s favorite.  As we can see from the look of horror on Helen’s face this favoritism is not cause for celebration.  The boss (a brilliant, menacing Sam Im – who also plays the cello beautifully) is a natural boor.  His insistent attentions terrify her.  Helen feels powerless to reject him, marrying him despite her loathing of his dirty jokes and small, wandering hands.

Helen seeks counsel from her mother, but as a woman worn down by life, Helen’s mother (Shelley Mitchell) is absorbed in her own sense of victim-hood.  Our hearts sink as we witness Helen crumbling under her husband’s will, in full “fight, flight, fear and fawn” mode.  The power of patriarchy is particularly evident when Helen is in the hospital after giving birth, traumatized and frozen.  Her nurse reassures in tense bright tone that Helen will love her baby once she holds it.  Her (male) doctor arrives to mansplain Helen’s feelings to her, and contradict the nurse’s instructions.  He shuts both of them down like it’s nothing.

The sun never shines in Machinal.  It is a world of grays and blacks.  Rochele Mac invokes this dark, enclosed world with 6 wooden desks, 6 desk lamps, and 6 wooden swivel chairs.   Colleen Doherty’s lighting is sharp and dramatic, punctuating key moments in rare flashes of color.  The extraordinary ensemble cast demonstrates a depth of talent as layered as Hahnji Jang’s gorgeous, textured, monochromatic costumes.  The actors move seamlessly among identities, under Seidel’s polished direction.  Helen’s lover (Soph Metcalf) serenading us, their voice smooth and beautiful, the French tune haunting.  Helen literally bedeviled by figures writhing around her in personification of her terror.  The rhythmic thump of a tap shoe that driving the opening of Act I.  (And the hoofing!  These tappers are hittin’!)

Act I responds more easily to the inside out treatment than Act II.   The scenes themselves are brief enough to leave space for movement and music.  It’s electric.  In Act II, Helen accompanies the office Telephone Girl (an adorable Kimberly Immanuel) to a smoky cabaret, where in an uncharacteristic act of daring, Helen says ‘yes’ to possibility.  Scenes of seduction follow, in filmic vignettes rather like like speed dating, as characters play a kind of musical chairs among the ‘cabaret tables.’  You feel the Weimar energy in these louche encounters.

Subsequently, however, the scenes as written are long and talky, which threatens to stop the action.  Another difficulty is that Helen spends the entire play in the same state of agitation.  She is given few levels to play, no moments to relax.  Winter is valiant doing the heavy lifting, but it’s tough.  The lengthy scene of Helen’s trial also presents a challenge.  Seidel leavens the (in)action  with a whirl of activity as Prosecution and Defense circle the witness box in which Helen sits, awaiting her fate.  The wait is worth it, however, as we are rewarded with a magical ending — a hint of a Pietà and exquisite music.

Machinal written by Helen Treadwell, directed by Amy Marie Seidel and choreographed by Madison Hilligoss.

With Katherine Winter, Temidayo Amay, Sam Im, Kimberly Immanuel, Soph Metcalf, Shelley Mitchell, Alice Reys, Veronica Simpson, Hannah Snow, Michael Verre, Alex Lauren and Annaliese Wilbur.  Scenic design by Rochele Mac, lighting design by Colleen Doherty, costume design by Hahnji Jang, sound design by Brittany Harris.

Presented by the New York Theatre Company, at New York City Center Stage II through July 13th.  Tickets HERE or go to https://www.nycitycenter.org.  Run time 2 hours 15 minutes with one intermission.

yoast_head_json.title: Machinal - The Front Row Center
yoast_head_json.description: MACHINAL -- New York Theatre Company’s revival of Machinal at New York City Center Theatre 2 is an extraordinary, revelatory dissection of a play about patriarchy and repression, as relevant today as when it was written in 1928.  The performance has a plasticity that blurs the lines between theater and spontaneous expression, creating theatrical poetry that is not to be missed.  It is one heck of an Off-Broadway debut.  Director Amy Marie Seidel and choreographer Madison Hilligoss honor the original text, capturing and building on its Expressionist roots through the interpolation of stylized gesture, sound, dance and music.  In so doing they have taken a wordy, static play and transformed it into a multi-dimensional, multi-disciplinary production that is yet laser focused.

@graph.description: MACHINAL -- New York Theatre Company’s revival of Machinal at New York City Center Theatre 2 is an extraordinary, revelatory dissection of a play about patriarchy and repression, as relevant today as when it was written in 1928.  The performance has a plasticity that blurs the lines between theater and spontaneous expression, creating theatrical poetry that is not to be missed.  It is one heck of an Off-Broadway debut.  Director Amy Marie Seidel and choreographer Madison Hilligoss honor the original text, capturing and building on its Expressionist roots through the interpolation of stylized gesture, sound, dance and music.  In so doing they have taken a wordy, static play and transformed it into a multi-dimensional, multi-disciplinary production that is yet laser focused.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

title.rendered: Henry VI by the Atlas Shakespeare Company

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

While finding their seats at the Chain Theatre, the audience was met with music—sometimes ominous, occasionally sublime—from the 16th century, echoing William Byrd’s Ave Verum Corpus with shadings of Claudio Monteverdi. How fitting that we should enter Shakespeare’s theatrical universe through the soundscape of his contemporaries, those lesser mortals who achieved mere competence. At the same time, our Will was busy inventing the human as we know it.

In this intimate black box theater on West 36th Street (a location that would have amused the Bard, who knew something about cramped performance spaces), Adriana Alter and her Atlas Shakespeare Company have accomplished something approaching the miraculous. They have breathed urgent, pulsing life into what academic pedants too often dismiss as Shakespeare’s “apprentice work”—as if genius ever truly served an apprenticeship to anyone but itself.

Why Henry VI Matters: The Anxiety of Influence Before the Influence

Shakespeare’s Unfashionable Masterpiece

The Henry VI trilogy has long languished in the shadow of Shakespeare’s mature histories, relegated to those academic footnotes where great works go to die a slow death by dissertation. Yet Alter’s company demonstrates with thrilling clarity—and here I must risk the wrath of the Shakespeare establishment—that these early plays contain, in wonderfully unrestrained form, all the psychological penetration and linguistic audacity that would eventually give us Lear’s heath and Hamlet’s Denmark.

What some scholars miss, bless their thorough souls, is that apprentice work from a genius is still genius. To witness this production is to observe the divine fire in its first flowering—raw, sometimes ungainly, but unmistakably touched by that cosmic force that separates Shakespeare from every other scribbler who ever presumed to hold a pen.

The Eternal Return of Political Chaos

What makes Henry VI critically relevant to our current carnival of political dysfunction is precisely what made it dangerous in Shakespeare’s time: it is a sustained meditation on the collapse of legitimate authority and the magnificent chaos that ensues when power divorces itself from wisdom. The titular king, portrayed with affecting vulnerability by Ned Bannon, represents something more troubling than mere weakness—he embodies the fundamental absurdity of inherited power in the face of human complexity.

Shakespeare, writing at the dawn of his career with that characteristic audacity of youth, was already grappling with questions that would obsess him unto death: What makes a king? What alchemical process transforms order into chaos? How do private ambitions, those delicious little malignancies of the soul, poison the public good? The young dramatist’s genius lay not in offering easy answers—Heaven knows we have enough of those—but in dramatizing their terrible, eternal urgency.

“Choose your side, take your chances!” Atlas Shakespeare Company presents Henry VI, directed by Adriana Alter, at the Chain Theater. Courtesy @atlasshakepeare on Instagram

Performance Excellence: When Actors Become Vessels for Genius

The Cast’s Wrestling Match with Immortal Language

The sixteen actors of Atlas Company rose magnificently to Shakespeare’s challenge, and what a challenge it is! To speak these lines is to risk everything—failure here is not merely dramatic but cosmic. William Oliver Watkins’s York crackled with the dangerous energy of a man discovering his capacity for evil, that moment when ambition first tastes blood and finds it sweet. Alexander Nero’s Gloucester embodied the tragic nobility of the faithful retainer, a man destroyed not by his vices but by his virtues—surely one of Shakespeare’s cruelest ironies.

Charlotte Blacklock’s Margaret revealed the steel beneath surface charm, prefiguring the she-wolf of later plays. Here, we see Shakespeare learning to write women who could devour their enemies with a smile—a skill that would serve him well when creating Lady Macbeth and Goneril.

The Delicious Corruption of Power

When Zachary C. Clark’s Suffolk declares that “Small things make base men proud,” we hear an early articulation of that profound understanding of human vanity that would later produce Iago and Edmund. The bishops’ meddling with royalty is not merely political opportunism but a manifestation of that universal human tendency to confuse personal ambition with divine mission. When Larry Reina’s Winchester schemes against Gloucester, we witness the eternal drama of envy disguised as righteousness—a performance so convincing that even the envious party believes his noble rhetoric.

Production Design: Visual Poetry in Service of Verbal Genius

Costume and Spectacle as Character

Nancy Nichols’s costume design immediately transported us into a world of medieval pageantry without sacrificing psychological realism—no mean feat when dealing with Shakespeare’s psychological realism, which tends to make mere historical accuracy seem quaint. The sight of Leah Schwartz’s Joan of Arc, resplendent in armor that caught the light with each gesture, embodied that fierce energy that makes this character one of Shakespeare’s most compelling early creations.

Ken Coughlin’s lighting and sound design created an atmosphere of perpetual uncertainty—the ominous rumble of military drums, blazing herald trumpets, the bright flash of steel in combat, and the way shadows fell across conspiratorial faces like moral judgments made visible. Joel Leffert’s fight choreography gave visceral weight to the play’s violence, reminding us that in Shakespeare’s world, political disputes are settled not through reasoned debate (what a quaint notion!) but through the honest brutality of bloodshed.

The Language of Early Genius: Abundance Before Restraint

Shakespeare’s Verbal Gluttony in All Its Glory

Perhaps the greatest pleasure of the evening was the opportunity to luxuriate in Shakespeare’s language in its early, untamed form. This is Shakespeare before he learned to restrain his exuberance and discovered that less could be more—though whether this discovery was gain or loss remains delightfully debatable. The result is a fertile abundance of metaphor, simile, and imagery that pleasures in its excess, like a young poet drunk on his first taste of real power over words.

When Talbot confesses that his thoughts are “whirled like a potter’s wheel,” we hear the young dramatist discovering metaphor’s power to illuminate psychological states. When Suffolk observes that “Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep,” we witness Shakespeare learning to embed profound truths in deceptively simple language. This skill would make him the most quotable writer in human history.

Picking of the Red and White Roses (Shakespeare, King Henry the Sixth, Part 1, Act 2, Scene 4), print, John Ogborne, after Josiah Boydell (MET, 42.119.547). Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication.

The Pithy Wisdom of Compressed Experience

The pithy quotes punctuate the evening—”True nobility is exempt from fear,” “Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven”—remind us why Shakespeare’s language has endured for four centuries while lesser poets moulder in libraries. These are not merely pretty phrases but compressed wisdom, insights into human nature crystallized in memorable form and delivered by actors who understand that Shakespearean language is not ornament but substance.

The Director’s Vision: Solving the Unsolvable

Adriana Alter’s Theatrical Alchemy

Adriana Alter’s expertise shines throughout this adaptation like a beacon in the darkness of contemporary theater. She has solved the considerable problem of condensing three sprawling plays into a single evening without sacrificing narrative coherence or emotional impact—a feat roughly equivalent to performing neurosurgery with a butter knife and making it look effortless.

Alter’s script maintains the essential structure of Shakespeare’s original while eliminating the repetitions and digressions that can make the complete trilogy feel unwieldy to modern audiences (we who have been trained by television to expect resolution every twelve minutes). Most importantly, she has preserved that urgent momentum that drives the best history plays—the feeling that events are spiraling toward an inevitable and terrible conclusion, much like the political moments of our collective memories.

Contemporary Relevance: The Eternal Return of Human Folly

Why These Medieval Kings Speak to Our Modern Chaos

What Shakespeare characterizes best in Henry VI are those human flaws that transcend any historical period: the tendency to mistake stubbornness for principle, the ease with which noble intentions justify ignoble actions, and the way personal grievances masquerade as public policy. Sound familiar? These characters speak to us today because they embody timeless patterns of human behavior—patterns we recognize with the uncomfortable shock of looking in a mirror after a sleepless night.

The marvelous plots and subplots that Alter’s adaptation preserved—the banishments and curses, the sword fights and murders, the jealousy and contempt—serve not as mere melodramatic ornaments but as external manifestations of internal conflicts. The “backstabbing sycophants” who populate this world are fascinating to watch because they embody, in exaggerated form, tendencies that exist in all of us. Their evil is seductive precisely because it is so thoroughly, recognizably human.

Genius Recognized and Celebrated

The Birth of English Drama’s Greatest Mind

In the end, what makes this production so successful is its recognition that Shakespeare’s early work deserves to be approached not as a historical curiosity or academic exercise but as a living drama. Henry VI plays may lack the perfect architecture of the mature tragedies—they have not yet learned to conceal their scaffolding—but they possess something equally valuable: the raw energy of a great imagination discovering its power.

To experience them in the intimate confines of the Chain Theatre, surrounded by actors who understand that Shakespeare’s language is not a museum piece but a vital force capable of illuminating the darkest corners of human experience, is to witness the birth of English drama’s greatest genius. This is Shakespeare in his “full, youthful vigor,” as producer Alexander Nero aptly phrases it, and it is absolutely glorious to behold—even when perhaps especially when it threatens to overwhelm us with its abundant humanity.

The Atlas Company has given us a rare chance to see a genius learning to be a genius. We should be grateful, for such opportunities are rarer than honest politicians and more precious than academic tenure. Don’t miss this show, theater lovers and literati! I enjoyed it immensely.

title.rendered: MAHABHARATA: DHARMA (PART 2) THE LIFE WE CHOOSE

content.rendered:
by Margret Echeverria

Okay, I practically ran to my seat to see the second half of this ancient story, MAHABHARATA: DHARMA (PART 2) THE LIFE WE CHOOSE created, written and directed by Miriam Fernandes and Ravi Jain at the Rose Theatre at Lincoln Center Jazz.  We are now entering the Bhagavad

Meher Pavri, Neil D’Souza and Anaka Maharaj-Sandhu in MAHABHRATA: DHARMA (PART 2) THE LIFE WE CHOOSE Photo by Lawrence Sumulong

Gita, many verses of which, to my surprise, are sung in a solo opera by the incomparable, Meher Pavri, whose soprano stylings put me into an ecstatic state.  And then, the role of Shiva in the battle itself is danced by Jay Emmanuel using choreography that is so off the hook it must have been dictated by Ram to Brandy Leary and Emmanuel as they conjure what can only be described as pure magic.  And Miriam Fernandes continues to guide us in storytelling crafted to make serious points about our human faltering – mainly repeating dark history as though we learn nothing in all our incarnations – as well as humor holding up a mirror to ourselves in the faces of these heroes and villains.  DHARMA (Part 2) also has some enhanced visuals with more video screens offering close ups of the actors on the stage in real time as well as psychodelic moving images which serve to open our minds to the spiritual messages woven into this epic.  Humanity and spirit are put as close to the viewer as possible.

Fernandes and Jain are masters at presenting all the layers available in the old text.  This is a soap opera on one level:  When the identity of Karna (Navtej Sandhu) is revealed to him, it feels like a scene from Days of our Lives.  We’re intrigued and excited by our empathy.  On another level: When Arjuna (Anaka Maharaj-Sandhu) faces the prospect of killing members of his own family, our morality is up and we are looking for a virtuous spiritual path out of the dilemma.  Maharaj-Sandhu empties a storehouse of emotions onto the stage evoking the anguish of our human condition as Krishna (Neil D’Souza), in form as Arjuna’s friend, tells him this is his Dharma; there’s no way out but through — dammit!!  This is a pivotal moment in the Bhagavad Gita that so many gurus have tried to explain to us.  Pavri, in form as consciousness, and D’Souza partner here to guide us into the spiritual realm and –  *wink* – it is a total trip.  I recommend absolute surrender, Kids.  Let it happen.  Everything becomes everything and we glimpse, as Arjuna sees, that we are a very small part of something so much bigger than us.  In all the destruction and all the grief and all the madness, there is a peace in being a piece of “the big something,” awareness of which is available to us at any time.

Arjuna’s own son, Abhimanyu, is lost in the battle.   We do not expect this as he is only fifteen years old.  Krishna allows a bending of truth to come from the mouth of Yudhishthira (Shawn Ahmed).  We certainly do not expect this as Krishna is the righteous Christ conciousness, is he not?  But sometimes we have to do the next right thing to preserve as much good as we can, don’t we?  Revelation follows deeper revelation for us to ponder for the rest of our lives, if we choose to do so.  And this is the point, I think.  I’ve pondered these last few days, influenced by this two-part production, the human compulsion to make promises and vows.  Perhaps these are not acts of generosity; rather, these pledges can be born of arrogance and ignorance as we do not possess a lens large enough to observe the entire universe and understand all its moving parts.  So much is hidden from us, that inserting ourselves ridged and immovable into the fabric of life can really tear at the tapestry.  As Bhishma (Sukania Venugopal) lays dying at the feet of the victorious Pandava brothers, Venugopal’s powerful voice places in our hearts not regret for the vow he made setting this whole ride into motion, but a sincere hope that we can come closer to enlightenment in our next incarnation.  If we come to earth again, we may be slightly better at just surrendering to what is rather than audaciously seeking to control outcomes.  Yet, judging as “bad” what we have done within a lifetime misses the lesson, too.

MAHABHARATA: DHARMA (PART 2) THE LIFE WE CHOOSE Created and written by Miriam Fernandes and Ravi Jain using poetry from Carole Satyamurti’s Mahabharata: A Modern Retelling, Directed by Ravi Jain with Associate Director Miriam Fernandes

WITH Shawn Ahmed (Yudhishthira), Neil D’Souza (Krishna), Jay Emmanuel (Shiva/Amba/Eklavya/Drupada), Miriam Fernandes (Associate Director, Storyteller), Ravin J. Ganatra (Dhritarashtra), Darren Kuppan (Duryodhana), Anaka Maharaj-Sandhu (Arjuna), Goldy Notay (Draupadi/Gandhari), Ellora Patnaik (Kunti/Drona), Meher Pavri (Voice of Krishna), Sakuntala Ramanee (Shakuni/Sanjaya), Ronica Sajnani (Standby – Dhritarashtra, Bhishma, Drona/Kunti), Ishan Sandhu (Standby – Shakuni/Sanjaya, Krishna, Arjuna), Navtej Sandhu (Karna/Satyavati), Munish Sharma (Bhima), Arun Varma (Standby – Karna, Bhima, Yudhishthira, Duryodhana), Sukania Venugopal (Bhishma)

MUSICIANS John Gzowski (Conductor, Co-Composer, Co-Sound Designer, Guitar), Suba Sankaran (Band Leader, Co-Composer, Co-Sound Designer, Voice), Dylan Bell (Bass, Keyboard, Music Contributions), Gurtej Singh Hunjan (Percussion, Music Contributions), Zaheer-Abbas Janmohamed (Tabla, Music Contributions), Hasheel Lodhia (Bansuri, Voice, Music Contributions)

Set Designer, Lorenzo Savoini; Costume Designer, Gillian Gallow; Lighting Designer, Kevin Lamotte; Associate Lighting Designer, Mikael Kangas; Projection Designer, Hana S. Kim; Associate Projection Designer, Ann Slote; Original Music & Sound Designer, John Gzowski & Suba Sankaran; Traditional Music Consultant, Hasheel Lodhia; Choreographer, Brandy Leary with contributions from Jay Emmanuel & Ellora Patnaik, Stage Manager, Neha Ross

This was a production included in Lincoln Center’s Summer for the City, Rose Theatre at Lincoln Center JAZZ @Columbus Circle, NYC.  The limited engagement ended June 29.

@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.
