title.rendered: Adam Pascal & Anthony Rapp: Celebrating Friendship & History

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

There’s nothing like watching two gifted, experienced performers – and good friends – enjoying themselves as they share their talent with an audience.  Adam Pascal and Anthony Rapp have returned to 54 Below to do just that, and the place is rockin.’  The pair perform a varied repertoire, exploring the territory between rock musical and rock music, singing songs from theatrical projects throughout their careers, as well as some of their favorite tunes.

Opening with U2 song “The Streets Have No Name” was a great way to draw us in.  The song has an irresistible, sweeping drama to it, which Rapp and Pascal capture beautifully.  Add to this the frustration of “Totally F—ked” from Spring Awakening and the passionate resolve in “One Song Glory” from Rent.  This is the start of the journey – dashing among nameless streets, determined to break free, with a dream to build a future and write one’s history.

This emotional journey wends its way through the entire set list – whether the subject is honoring our choices, moving on, looking back at accomplishments or contemplating life’s myriad obstacles.  It’s all there in the music.  What gets us through, again and again, are the ties that bind.  For Pascal and Rapp, their 30 year friendship, dating from when they both starred in the original cast of Rent, has been key.

“There is no future, there is no past. I live this moment as my last.
There’s only us. There’s only this. Forget regret, or life is yours to miss.”

One of the highlights of the evening was the cover of the David Bowie/Freddie Mercury duet “Under Pressure” (which at this point could be our national anthem…)  Pascal and Rapp do full justice to the emotion and the range (both vocal and textural) of the piece.  Jump to their delightful spoof of the candle duet from Rent – played for laughs with a wicked gleam in their eyes.  Rapp and Pascal play so well off each other.  They are generous performers, whose camaraderie reads effortlessly across the footlights.

The band really delivers as well, with Lee Moretti on guitar, Paul Gill on bass, and Jerry Marotta on drums.  Musical director Daniel Weiss leads from the piano.  The show is a rock and roll loud, and the band sometimes overwhelms the singers, but sound balance is tricky at the best of times.

People really connected to this entire show.  Table of adoring fans singing along to tunes from Rent, cheering after every song, ready to follow whatever road Rapp and Pascal decided to go down.  From the life affirming “I’ve Loved These Days” by Billy Joel to a quiet interlude of “Fake Plastic Trees” by Radiohead, to Peter Gabriel to Broadway, Rapp and Pascal can sing it all.

As the evening drew to a close, Pascal brought the house down with a gutsy rendition of the blues tune “When I’m Down” by Chris Cornell, creating the kind of magic you only experience in live performance, and for which an audience lives.

“You’re living in America
At the end of the millennium
You’re living in America
Where it’s like the Twilight Zone.”

Remember when we had no idea what would happen to our computers when the clock ticked past midnight?  Well we survived the Millennium, but I think we can all safely say we are still living in the Twilight Zone.  So what to do?  Celebrate.  Celebrate friendship.  Honor history.  Celebrate gratitude.  Thus the journey ended with a beginning.  “Seasons of Love” with its heartfelt, nostalgic tone, reminds us to treasure loved ones.  True friendship binds us closer over time, helps us to gain in wisdom, and guides our resolve to build a better future.  You can’t beat that.

Adam Pascal & Anthony Rapp:  Celebrating Friendship & History, at 54 Below (254 West 54th St.) June 24th to July 6th.  Tickets available HERE or call (646) 476-3551.

In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Duke & Roya, now playing at the Lucille Lortel, is a romcom (two people from different worlds, Stephanie Nur (Roya) and Jay Ellis (Duke), struggling to come together), riding on the backs of a historical reflection of the American presence in Afghanistan. It moves between 2015 and 2025 and packs a punch in the depth of development and growth that each character experiences throughout the play.

The theme of how we cover up who we really are, Roya: girl/boy, Duke: gangsta rapper/raised well-to-do with all the advantages, US presence in Afghanistan: hero/back-stabbing traitor, is strongly felt in each character and leads to their vulnerability and personal growth throughout the play.

The first act is a lot of exposition, letting the audience know the war-torn world that they’ve just entered and a little bit of its history, the young lovers discovering each other and us them, and the parents looking out for their children. After all this groundwork has been laid, the second act is a tight exploration of feelings and emotional revelations that make for good theater.

To promote his second hip-hop album, Duke’s (Jay Ellis) publicist has arranged for him to perform a public service gig entertaining the troops in Afghanistan. He arrives as a naive, innocent kid, unawares of the reality he is entering, and is assigned an interpreter, Roya (Stephanie Nur), a young, strong-minded Afghan woman. She has achieved her position as one of the top interpreters, having lived the practice of bacha pose. If a family does not have a son, a daughter is chosen to live the life of a boy until puberty hits and she can no longer pass. This practice granted her the freedom and education opportunities that women are not allowed to experience, but ultimately, she was forced back from those freedoms when she had to return to being a girl. Living in two worlds gave her a passion for women’s rights as she personally experienced, “Everything as a boy, nothing as a girl.”

When Duke sees Roya for the first time, he is smitten and works nonstop to win her over. He even convinces her to accompany him off base for an adventure, which, of course, is strictly against the rules. And as is to be expected, something bad happens, which brings in Duke’s mother (the phenomenal Noma Dumezweni) and Roya’s father (the charming Dariush Kashani) into the mix as the young lovers deal with their feelings, loyalties, and the pragmatic situation of their lives.

The actors Noma and Dariush take their fair share of the spotlight and at times, through their personal charm, eclipse the main characters so much so that the play could be called Duke & Roya (and Desiree and Sayeed).

Though not a complete meal, Duke & Roya is a very satisfying evening at the theatre.

—–

Duke & Roya, was written by Charles Randolph-Wright, and directed by Warren Adams.

Actors: Jay Ellis, Stephanie Nur, Noma Dumezweni, Dariush Kashani

Original music by Ronve O’Daniel, Scenic design by Wilson Chin, Costume Design by Snowber Sabrina Spanta, Lighting design by Amina Alexander, Projection design by Caite Hevner, Sound design and additional music by Taylor J. Williams

Lucille Lortel Theatre, 121 Christopher St, New York, NY 10014, USA

Tickets $79, but rush tickets are available for $39 for every performance on the TodayTix app. Rush will open at 9am each morning and will be available until 2 hours before the performance, or when no seats remain.

The show’s running time is 2 hours and 20 minutes, including one 15-minute intermission. Smoke and explosions are utilized.

title.rendered: Mahabharata: Karma (Part 1) The Life We Inherit

content.rendered:
By Margret Echeverria

When we were small, we slept the sleep of innocents.  Bedtime fables of royal figures, lucky plebians, gods and talking animals muted our fears by placing them in time and lands far far away.  As grown ups, lessons in those tales can evolve into our philosophies. MAHABHARATA: KARMA (PART 1) THE LIFE WE INHERIT created and written by Miriam Fernandes and Ravi Jain now playing at Lincoln Center’s Rose Theater is a modern re-telling of ancient sanskrit messages of love, revenge, trickery and battles to the death.  It is a thrill to just let it consume us and slightly mute the reality of present troubles.  I say “slightly” because the familiar myths, symbols, and themes reinvented here in dance, ritual story-telling and humor evoke both collective pain and hope for our increasingly loud world.

The influence of Anne Bogart on the production’s co-creator, Miriam Fernandes, is felt as the bodies of the actors animate the story.  Almost all the action in the first act of Part 1 takes place inside a small circle of red sand on the stage, yet the actors’ movements expand inside that circle representing the reach this story can have into our psyches.  The Mahabharata brings us into a world where a promise is to be honored even when it is inconvenient; a world in which the destiny of human beings – even those with superhero powers, like the mighty warrior, Arjuna, Anaka Maharaj-Sandhu – is often pre-determined.  Fernandes begins the naration in the middle of the story with Arjuna being tricked by Agni into burning down Arjuna’s newly acquired asset,  Khāṇḍava Forest.  The vast woods burn for fifteen days carrying a cloak of smoke over truth and generational curses far into the future.  Maharaj-Sandhu is a beautiful and graceful Arjuna, the third of five Pandava brothers born of royal blood.   The Pandavas have one hundred first cousins in the Kaurava family sired by their father’s brother.  Duryodhana, Darren Kuppan, the eldest of 100, is like an an addict who, if he would only hit bottom, would give us a feeling of divine schadenfreude.  On the Pandava side, Arjuna’s older brother, Yudhishthira, Shawn Ahmed, is ambitious, but has a fateful gambling problem.  Ahmed embodies the beloved addicted friend whom we would beg to go to a cosmic twelve-step meeting.  Alas, Yudhishthira’s habit and pride lose the Pandava’s kingdom to the Kaurava cousins in a game of dice.

Fernandes and Ravi Jain boldly bring traditional lore, rich with layered messages and meaning, to confront our present Western-dominated world.  Characters are gender fluid, feminine wisdom and pleasure are emphasized – Draupadi, Goldy Notay, is a happy adored wife of Arjuna and his brothers! – and favoring one’s own children over the children of others is an act against dharma.  The disagreements and jealousy between the two families becomes a rivalry.  If the signs of the gods and wisdom of the ancestors were not ignored by mortal egos, a period of  peace and abundance would have prevailed.   Bhishma, Sukania Venugopal, is a wise elder who is stubborn and a party-pooper.  However, the other characters’ refusal to take heed of Bhishma’s wisdom is the fuel for yhe ever-widening fire devouring this family.  Human ego does not perceive that everything is everything else, everything influences everything everywhere, time is anything but linear and we are all family even if we don’t like each other.  How shameful that we still choose war with our adversaries in 2025.  We are still stuck.  Bless us all.

I loved the adorable and sassy Ellora Patnaik  as Kunti, Arjuna’s mama, who has a little secret that incarnates as Karna, Munish Sharma, becoming a huge threat to peace.  Sharma is perfectly cast feeling twice as tall as Patnaik and moving with commanding steady precision on the stage.  Patnaik’s dancing is a whimsical frenzy that becomes hypnotic – she glamours our purview away from her deception.  That is not the only magic happening here; the music of John Gzowski and Suba Sankaran moving through the piece is absolutely transcendent.  The star of Part 1 is Fernandes, who’s cerebral commitment and physical power as she guides us through this story is indefatigable.  We will walk into the fire with her.  The perfect red sand circle from the first act is dispersed over the stage through the chaos of the conflict in the second.  And we are left at the end of Part 1 as breathless as we are contemplative.  I can hardly wait to see Part 2.  I recommend you go see Part 1 ASAP, and I’ll see you on the flip side!

MAHABHARATA: KARMA (PART 1) THE LIFE WE INHERIT Created and written by Miriam Fernandes and Ravi Jain using poetry from Carole Satyamurti’s Mahabharata: A Modern Retelling, Directed by Ravi Jain with Associate Director Miriam Fernandes

WITH Shawn Ahmed (Yudhishthira), Neil D’Souza (Krishna), Jay Emmanuel (Shiva/Amba/Eklavya/Drupada), Miriam Fernandes (Associate Director, Storyteller), Ravin J. Ganatra (Dhritarashtra), Darren Kuppan (Duryodhana), Anaka Maharaj-Sandhu (Arjuna), Goldy Notay (Draupadi/Gandhari), Ellora Patnaik (Kunti/Drona), Meher Pavri (Voice of Krishna), Sakuntala Ramanee (Shakuni/Sanjaya), Ronica Sajnani (Standby – Dhritarashtra, Bhishma, Drona/Kunti), Ishan Sandhu (Standby – Shakuni/Sanjaya, Krishna, Arjuna), Navtej Sandhu (Karna/Satyavati), Munish Sharma (Bhima), Arun Varma (Standby – Karna, Bhima, Yudhishthira, Duryodhana), Sukania Venugopal (Bhishma)

MUSICIANS John Gzowski (Conductor, Co-Composer, Co-Sound Designer, Guitar), Suba Sankaran (Band Leader, Co-Composer, Co-Sound Designer, Voice), Dylan Bell (Bass, Keyboard, Music Contributions), Gurtej Singh Hunjan (Percussion, Music Contributions), Zaheer-Abbas Janmohamed (Tabla, Music Contributions), Hasheel Lodhia (Bansuri, Voice, Music Contributions)

Set Designer, Lorenzo Savoini; Costume Designer, Gillian Gallow; Lighting Designer, Kevin Lamotte; Associate Lighting Designer, Mikael Kangas; Projection Designer, Hana S. Kim; Associate Projection Designer, Ann Slote; Original Music & Sound Designer, John Gzowski & Suba Sankaran; Traditional Music Consultant, Hasheel Lodhia; Choreographer, Brandy Leary with contributions from Jay Emmanuel & Ellora Patnaik, Stage Manager, Neha Ross

Lincoln Center’s Summer for the City, Rose Theatre at Lincoln Center JAZZ @Columbus Circle, NYC  Pay What You Can Tickets Here

Thursday, June 26 At 7:30 PM, Saturday, June 28 At 2:00 PM, Sunday, June 29 At 2:00 PM

excerpt.rendered: Fernandes and Ravi Jain boldly combine tradition, rich with layered messages and meaning, with struggles of our modern Western-dominated world.  Characters are gender fluid, feminine wisdom and pleasure are emphasized – Draupadi, Goldy Notay, is a happy adored wife of Arjuna and his brothers! – and favoring one’s own children over the children of others is an act against dharma.  The disagreements and jealousy between the two families becomes a rivalry that could have been avoided if the signs of the gods and wisdom of the ancestors were not ignored by mortal egos.   How shameful that we still choose war and we have not found a better way to take care of one another in 2025.  Ego does not see that everything is everything else and influences everything everywhere and time is anything but linear.  We are still stuck, but we are still trying.  Bless us all.

@graph.description: In the summer of 1978, while watching a performance of A Murder is Announced on the London stage, Margret fell in love with the theatre. Born and raised in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Margret came to New York City in 1994. She was admitted to Newmyn’s Nose Limitless Theatre Limited, an innovative and award winning improvisational company, in the summer of 1995 and eventually became a member of the company’s board. Margret starred in the critically acclaimed short film Jigsaw Venus by Dean Capsalis in 2000 (Best Actress, Buenos Aires International Independent Film Festival) and her film career was begun. She played the adorable Fag Hag (GenX does not find this term offensive at all), Audrey, in both A Four Letter Word (2007) as well as Violet Tendencies (2010), films by Casper Andreas and Jesse Archer. She has a co-starring role in Max Emerson's film, Hooked. Always sentimental about performing for a live audience, Margret penned and performed Orangerie, a one-woman show exploring the subject of finding love while traveling non-traditional avenues, which premiered at the Bowery Poetry Club in November of 2005 and ran through the spring of 2006 to critical acclaim. After Margret’s family survived the death of their son, Gavin, to SIDS in 2011, she penned her last one woman show, Finding Gavin, which premiered in New York City in 2015. She was on the season finale of Law & Order SVU in 2021. Margret studied Acting at Regent’s College in London, Classical Voice and Opera at the Royal Academy of Music in London, and Acting at Sally Johnson Studio here in New York City. She has a BFA in Acting from Rockford University. Margret is also a published poet. She lives in Yonkers, NY with her daughter, Alyson.

title.rendered: Paul Taylor Dance Company Returns to The Joyce Theater

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

The Paul Taylor Dance Company returned to The Joyce Theater for their two-program production from July 17-22. The program features two early masterworks—Tablet (1960) and Churchyard (1969)—newly reconstructed for the first time in decades. Brought back with care by an intergenerational team, including original cast members, led by Artistic Director Michael Novak, these rarely seen works were performed alongside Cloven Kingdom (1976), Polaris (1976), and the 50th anniversary of Esplanade.

The Paul Taylor Dance Company run at The Joyce each summer is always a wonderful, much anticipated evening, as the diversity and creativity of each piece always surprise me. The ease of shifting tones shown through music and lighting, especially this year, highlighted the not just the interpretation of the dance but the storytelling of each piece.

TABLET

Photo by Steven Pisano

Tablet, in both Programs A and B, is a playful duet of shaping movements that both bring the dancers together and make the audience chuckle. One performer’s costumed in a blue unitard with a face painted as a completely white circle. The other, in a golden yellow, has her face instead outlined in white. Their costuming and dance play with shape, and movement to convey emotion, and the configuration of their bodies both apart and as one add a fun, clowning element to the performance.

FEATURING: Kristin Draucker & Devon Louis.

Music by David Hollister; Choreography by Paul Taylor; Designer Ellsworth Kelly; Lighting by Jennifer Tipton; Set reconstructed by Santo Loquasto; Kristin Draucker Devon Louis.

POLARIS

Polaris in itself was a unique performance as the single piece was divided into two parts. While the choreography was the same in both Part I and Part II, the cast, lighting, music, and individual interpretations heavily contrasted. The change in music and lighting highlights the significant shift in tone, and it does feel as though they are two separate entities lacing each other.

Photo by Whitney Browne

FEATURING: Lee Duveneck Alex Clayton, John Harnage, Lisa Borres Casey, Jada Pearman, Jake Vincent, Jessica Ferretti, Gabrielle Barnes, Emmy Wildermuth, and Payton Primer.

Music Composed for the Dance by Donald York; Choreography by Paul Taylor; Set and Costumes by Alex Katz; Lighting by Jennifer Tipton.

CLOVEN KINGDOM

Photo by Paul B. Goode

Men costumed in tuxedos and women costumed in contemporary, airy dresses leap across the stage; but mirrored shapes strapped around their heads, and over their faces add an eccentric and stunning element to this piece. The mirrors seeimingly absorb and cast strobes of white light across the stage, the audience, the walls surrounding us all. It is the most memorable performance of the evening–almost robotic, in the way the metal and glass lift the performers upwards as they leap (they stay perfectly positioned on top their heads), moving them from one end of the stage to the other, time and time again.

FEATURING: Jessica Ferretti, Gabrielle Barnes, Emmy Wildermuth, Elizabeth Chapa, Devon Louis, John Harnage, Shawn Lesniak, Austin Kelly, Kristin Draucker, Lisa Borres Casey, Jada Pearman, Payton Primer.

Music by Arcangelo Corelli, Henry Cowell and Malloy Miller; Combined by John Herbert McDowell, Choreography by Paul Taylor, Women’s Costumes by Scott Barrie, Headpieces by John Rawlings, Lighting by Jennifer Tipton.

CHURCHYARD

Churchyard places us in what I imagine as a cemetery; the browns and rust cotumed dancers remind me of ground, dirt, rock, burials. The lighting is altered as performers alternate between nuns and priests and the darker, eerier parts of the churchyard.

Photo by Steven Pisano

 

Photo by Steven Pisano

FEATURING: Alex Clayton, John Harnage, Lisa Borres Casey, Shawn Lesniak, Jake Vincent, Jessica Ferretti, Emmy Wildermuth, Elizabeth Chapa, Payton Primer.

Music by Cosmos Savage (based on authentic medieval pieces), Choreography by Paul Taylor, Designer Alec Sutherland, Lighting by Jennifer Tipton.

ESPLANADE

Esplanade feels like the joy of warm weather. Forms of movement are showcased: dancers are costumed in oranges and pinks; they leap, run across the stage, leap over each other. They carefully stand on and lift each other. Hues deepen as lights dim to express the deeper, slower movements. Dancers come together into a circle, their movements become one as their bodies connect.

Photo by Steven Pisano

FEATURING: Kristin Draucker, Lee Duveneck, Devon Louis, Lisa Borres Casey, Jada Pearman, Jessica Ferretti, Austin Kelly, Gabrielle Barnes, Elizabeth Chapa.

Music by Johann Sebastian Bach:
Violin Concerto in E Major, Double Concerto for Two Violins in D Minor (Largo & Allegro)

Choreography by Paul Taylor, Costumes by John Rawlings, Lighting by Jennifer Tipton.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall
“Trophy Boys” is the latest in the lineup of exciting theatre that will challenge you.  Or challenge somebody.  Like a congressional rep for instance.  Or Trump.  Well, ANYTHING is a challenge for Trump so perhaps that is low bar.  When I heard his declaration that there would be two sexes only going forward all I would think was, “Well that horse left the barn a long time ago.”  Never mind the centuries of cultures where there was a blurring of gender rolls.  Our recent history is proof that that gender is fluid – no matter the Big Beautiful declarations.
Trophy Boys is an investigation of gender both on and offstage.  The Australian playwright Emmanuelle Mattana lays out the thesis that “Gender is learnt, which means it can also be taught.”  Having spent some years at a private Australian secondary school, Mattana watched as “argument turned into sport… Logic was a game.”  The purpose was to decimate the other side even if you did not believe in your own argument.
In other words, Debate was a lead up to war.  Not that any of the elite boys would go to war, but they would be the leaders who sent people into battle.
From the minute these boys David (Terry Hu), Jared (Louisa Jacobson), Scott (Esco Jouléy), and Owen (Emmanuelle Mattana) enter their prep room we know they are gearing up for a battle.  Their subject is revealed when the envelope is opened – “Feminism has failed women.”  This team is to argue in the affirmative.
Instead of being surprised or shocked in any way, they do what they always do. They get to work.  5 minutes of silent brainstorming and then the ideas ricochet around the room.  This is where Mattana’s writing shines.  The ideas are deep and dense.   Feminism has locked women into new specific roles that are no less limiting than the old one.  Feminism has reshaped women’s contribution and at the same time has weakened men by creating gray areas of behavior where no one wins.  Back and forth they go, new ideas springing forth like weeds.  Each boy has his own specialty and they defer to one another as the arguments strengthen.  Stats, history, logic and of course subterfuge – because they will do what they have to – each boy has a role to play.
They have an exact amount of time for prep and are not allowed to use their devices.  Pads and writing implements only.
Until they stumble.  And a big stumble it is.  An enormous fly is splatted into the ointment.  In a nanno-second an outside accusation enters the room and pulls an invisible plug.  Instead of full steam ahead, these boys are adrift and their sails are limp.  Is it still one for all?  Or has it changed to something closer to “Lord Of The Flies”?  We watch the current shift.  The outcome is never certain.  Except we do know that winning is still the goal.  No matter the other team is all female and one of the members is Jared’s girlfriend.  She can be sacrificed.  As a matter of fact so can any one of the team members, if needs be.
This is where the story gets a bit long in the tooth.  Mattana’s writing tries to be all things to all people.  Where a laser incision might have done the job, the writing becomes general.  Instead of zeroing in on a story line, the writing becomes diffuse. We get lost in the fog when what we are looking for is clarity.
One by one the foibles of each boy are revealed as possible causes of the accusation. In addition to questioning each other they must consider that the accusation itself is false.  The accuser is anonymous and the accusation vague.    No one is safe.  The onion is peeled into within an ugly inch of its core.  These are not stories we want to hear.  These are not stories these boys want known, but they will latch onto on each other’s reputations and weaknesses with no hesitation.  Until there is no more time left.
When the time runs out they leave the prep room to do what they have been trained to do – cover each other’s butt and win.  The truth remains vague and the battle unfought.  A disappointing non-resolution for us, but one that is probably closer to reality.  Life is messy and these kids are being trained to navigate the waters created by them that have the goods or at least own them.
Keep watch, my friends.  We are the ones with our hands on the throttle.  There is no THEY.
TROPHY BOYS by Emmanuelle Mattana, Directed by Danya Taymor
WITH Terry Hu, Louisa Jacobson, Esco Jouléy, and Emmanuelle Mattana
Scenic design by Matt Saunders, costume design by Márion Talán de la Rosa, lighting design by Cha See
Through July 27 at MCC, 515 W. 52 Street.  Tickets HERE

By Tulis McCall

If you are looking for a little optimism, look no further than John Philip in his most recent cabaret presentation, “Say Yes”.  Using classics from the American Songbook, as well as new lyrics by his co-creator and director Marilyn Maye, Philip gives us his upbeat version of life in the here and now and kicks off Pride Week in style.

Not an easy task in today’s political climate.

Philip is a man of a Certain Age, so when he tells you that he was a participant in the early Gay Parades – before the word PRIDE was attached to any activity – you better believe him.  Back in the day, as many of you remember, being gay was illegal in some circles and at the very least frowned upon in most.  Philip glosses over the mean spirited folks to focus on the people who became a support system.  People who became friends.  And one gets the feeling that as he looks us up and down he is ready to add more friends to his roster.

Not only does Philip greet us with open arms, he doles out philosophy.  Like his mentor, Marilyn Maye, he is an optimist.  Specifically he is an optimist with original lyrics at the ready.  So smooth are the added lyrics that this writer was unaware they were new.  I still can’t tell you exact new lines, but that is what the press release said!  And Philip never misses a beat.  “Today I Love Everybody”  (Harold Arlen and Dorothy Fields) leads off the parade.  Followed by “Let Me Sing a Funny Song”  (Irving Berlin) made famous by Al Jolson.  There is an amusing medley of songs referring to dancing, which Philip refuses to demonstrate, thereby sparing us all.

Not everything is sparkling and glowing.  There are the break-ups and the disappointments.  A moving blend of “Walk On By”  (Hal David and Burt Bachrach), “I Don’t Remember You” (John Kander and Fred Ebb), a novel twist on the classic “By The Time I Get To Phoenix” (Jimmy Webb) and “Isn’t This Better?” (Kander and Ebb) takes us through the complicated tunnel of relationships.  Philip completes the evening with a tribute to being on the water as a sailor – and makes you believe that the sea is second home for him.

He closes with “Old Friends” (Sondheim) and “The Secret of Life” (James Taylor) both of which sounded as though they had been touched by the loving hands of Ms. Maye. The cherry on top is the superb trio accompanying Mr. Philip: David Pearl, Pianist/Music Director, Dan Gross, drummer and Tom Hubbard, bassist.

John Philip and David Pearl; Photo by Michael Lee Stever.

Philip closes the evening with an act of grace and generosity.  Marilyn Maye joins him and gives us three of her most iconic songs “Golden Rainbow,” “Being Alive,” and “Here’s To Life” by Walter Marks, Stephen Sondheim and Artie Butler/ Phyllis Molinary respectively.)

All in all this is a sweet evening.  While not an astonishing vocalist, Mr. Philip possesses a heart filled with Courage, Love and Hope that he happily shares with all of us with each song.  We leave his show feeling uplifted.  Who among us c old  not use a little more of that?

One night only at The Iridium.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Kendra  Jones

Taylor Mac’s writing, coupled with Darko Tresnjak‘s direction, in Prosperous Fools is sharp, and infiltrated with bizarre sets and humor which is just as absurd—and certainly not subtle.

Inspired by “Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme,” Prosperous Fools pokes fun at both the middle-class, the vain, and the “average” audience of the arts making attempts to climb in social status. Whether it’s the director of a high-profile arts organization, such as the ballet company shown in Prosperous Fools, events to raise money bring thousands, and millions, of dollars to these non-profits, enabling them to remain operable.

Should billionaires decide what’s seen?

An artist (Taylor Mac) and artistic director (Jennifer Regan) place us in the center of gala walk-through for the 2025 National Ballet Theatre. It’s overwhelming. It’s chaotic.

Photo by Travis Emery Hackett

The ensemble of dancers–muses–are a mix of gender and body type; they rehearse for their dance at the gala, and their rehearsal is just as laughable as the production itself. They warm up at a small barre, set in center stage; one dancer becomes chained in shackles, others mark their steps, folding into each other in a small circle. A red braided rope on entrails is pulled from the shackled muse.

The role we accept and clearly allow philanthropy to play in the arts is put center stage as billionaire, $#@%$ (Jason O’Connell), (yes, referred to in a voice note and denoted as a line of symbols), is involved for the fame and money. As if the theater’s artistic director is any better. We are forced to face the truth of not-for-profit arts organizations, especially when the potential for money is at stake. Musical notes are used to bleep out names and places, making it both obvious and comical who, what, and where the writing is referring to.

Photo by Travis Emery Hackett

Sierra Boggess, most known from her performance as Ariel in The Little Mermaid and Christine Daaé in The Phantom of the Opera, joins the cast as movie star-turned humanitarian (####).

A pot-bellied child caked in mud and clothed in dirty rags, takes the stage smiling, grateful to be used as a prop and arm candy to #### (Sierra Boggess), the gala’s movie star-turned-humanitarian. It’s clear who #### symbolizes, and somehow we are laughing at this pathetic scene. And $#@%$ will take it upon himself to do anything he can with this humanitarian to further himself financially and socially.

Photo by Travis Emery Hackett

The art itself within this production, from the setup of the gala, the props seen as magnificent, and the dancing itself, is mocked.

It’s like we are at a parade of fools, one after the other—philanthropist, humanitarian (Sierra Boggess) artistic director, artist, the muses themselves, and intern, right down to the arts audience dressed in anything from formal attire to athletic clothing—we’re all made fun of. Mac is endearing in his own passion for the arts and brave in his unapologetic honesty. We see the work dancers put into their craft—and the hours of rehearsals to being cast aside as soon as the real act of the night enters the space.

Act 2 brought the absurd to the next level. Prosperous Fools, in its entirety is too long; while the production can keep screaming at us and making us laugh at essentially ourselves, and those we look up to, it does more in its lines of humor and stage direction than its time on stage. The intermission left a stagnant feeling upon returning to the the theater. Though, seeing the significant set change–a red carpet morphed into a bloodied sheep and a blood-splattered blow-up pool–was quite stirring. The foreshadowing of the progressively-more gruesome production led us to the level of ridiculous Taylor Mac can execute perfectly.

While the production is slow at parts, and ventures into laughably inappropriate and ludicrous after intermission, I walk away asking myself, what did I just watch? But knowing fully well what has just transpired is what we see live and televised for awards shows, benefits, any-scale events to raise money for a not-for-profit. It’s the absurd lengths we’ll go to obtain financial profit, and social gain. It’s sick, wild, and true; Mac is an artist brave enough to admit it, present the complexities of philanthropy, and force the audience of all classes to ask ourselves the level of hypocrisy we will simply look past to get ahead.

But if you think there is no thicket,

Consider how you got your ticket,

And whose excluded from this show.

For who can pay, is who can go.

And who can go, is who partakes

And who partakes, is who then makes

The rules, based on their own reflections,

And so we’re kept within our sections.

Rather than the cast taking their bows while the audience claps, we filter into the lobby as the Artist mops the mess on stage.

 

Written by and Starring Taylor Mac. Directed by Darko Tresnjak.

CAST: Sierra Boggess (####-####), Kaliswa Brewster (Intern), Aerina Park Deboer (Pot-Bellied Child), Megumi Iwama (Muse #2), Jason O’Connell ($#@%$), Ian Joseph Paget (Prometheus), Taylor Mac (Artist), Jennifer Regan (Philanthropoid), Cara Seymour (Muse #3), Jennifer Smith (Stage Manager), Em Stockwell (Muse #1).

Udi Gershuni (Conductor/Keyboard), Ronen Itzik (Percussian), Taya Ricker (Violin).

CREATIVE TEAM:

Oran Eldor (Music), Austin McCormick (Choreograper), Alexander Dodge (Scenic Designer), Anita Yavich (Costume Designer), Matthew Richards (Lighting Designer), Jane Shaw (Sound Designer), Aaron Rhyne (Projection Designer), Rocio Mendez (Fight and Intimacy Choreographer), Andrew Wade (Voice Director), Tom Watson (Hair & Wig Designer), Jonno Knust (Properties Supervisor), Jonathan Kalb (Production Dramaturg).

Shane Schnetzler (Production Stage Manager), Sammy Landau (Assistant Stage Manager), Ian Joseph Paget (Fight Captain), Cara Seymour (Dance Captain).

The running time is 2 hours, including a 15-minute intermission.

Prosperous Fools runs until June 29, at Scripps Main Stage, Polonsky Shakespeare Center, 262 Ashland Place Brooklyn, NY 11217. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Hot Sardines is one of the best old-time jazz bands I have enjoyed seeing. Many of you may know them from their sold-out Joe’s Pub shows, and they bring that magic to the Birdland stage and making the room come alive from the first note. They are a celebration of the music of the early 20th century and a celebration of us, where we’ve been and how that relates to where we are now. Their music is rejoicing in life, in sound, in stories. An extraordinary ensemble, like water flowing in a stream, all going in the same direction but some parts splashing over rocks, some parts pausing in pools, and other parts rushing madly to the sea. All one in perfect harmony!

The Hot Sardines formed in 2007 with Miz Elizabeth Bougerol, vocalist and washboard, and Evan Palazzo, band leader and pianist, who played free gigs for friends and flash mobs.  And with that, The Hot Sardines have created an almost cult following of tweens, teens, millennials, and boomers. All drawn to their slide style of jazz that had the audience tapping their feet, swaying to the beat, and swagger that this ensemble created.

They opened the evening with the classic “Love Potion #9,” encouraging the packed house at Birdland to join in. And we all did. They had the whole audience in the palm of their hands from the very first note. That doesn’t happen too often. The richness of each song they played comes with a natural ease. I use the word ease, but I also want to note that they are HOT! Hot and tight like a can of tightly packed sardines drenched in a tangy sauce, just ready for the tasting.

Ms. Elizabeth Bougerol’s voice is smooth and sweet with a beauty to it that is statuesque in its power. Their Oscar Hammerstein II and Romburg’s “Lover Come Back To Me” rocked the room with the trombone and flute duet being a force unto itself. Speaking of force, the surprising bass and ukulele duet had me floored, and a “member” of their percussion section, the jazz tap dancer Lamont Brown, with his feet on fire moving in and out of the ensemble, was a wonder unto himself.

They are telling tales with both words and music, and we are following along with every moment of the narrative. The music often had people out of their chairs and standing. Some took advantage of their tables being in the back of Birdland’s multi-level space and got up and danced. THEY DANCED!!! IN THE AISLES!!! AT BIRDLAND!!! That I have never witnessed in the many shows I’ve been to. That was the crowd’s reaction to The Hot Sardines on a wonderful night in June.

Their tribute to Quincy Jones, “Into Each Life Some Rain Must Fall,” was a beautiful rearranging of the song that I know Mr. Jones would have loved. Then there was the timeless “St. James Infirmary” that opened with a trombone singing in a way that only a trombone can. I do believe that the trombone is one of the only musical instruments that can talk. It speaks in its stunning language, and we become all ears to the conversation.

It was a splendid evening at Birdland. If you missed The Hot Sardines this time around, do not fret, they have a running gig at Birdland every six months, and they seem to be playing somewhere all the time (show schedule HERE)! So, look to Birdland in December, and everywhere else until then. I believe there’s no better way to spend the holidays than with The Hot Sardines for a guaranteed wonderful evening.

Birdland Jazz Club 315 W 44th St, New York, NY 10036

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

I don’t quite know how to describe Bear Grease.  It’s a musical theater / night club act / video show all jumbled together.  It has appeal, but it’s overly ambitious, unfocused and definitely niche.

Co-created in Treaty 6 Territory in Alberta (Canada) by husband and wife writing team LightningCloud (Crystle Lightning and Henry Cloud Andrade),  Bear Grease weaves cultural elements from various indigenous nations into the narrative of the popular musical Grease, adding an indigenous ‘voice’ to an American musical theater classic.  Given the experience of first nations peoples in the 1950’s, the choice of material fractures an already fractured fairy tale (in a good way). The cast also sing a variety of other 1950’s oldies but goodies.

Grease showcases a culture doing its best to hide the cracks behind the image of idyllic (meaning:  white, middle class, suburban) life in 1950’s America.  It satirizes the rewards of conformity in twinsets and motorcycle jackets.  Girls gotta be bad to be good.  Guys gotta conform to make good.  The action plays for comedy, in the risk-free environment of nostalgia, but its narrative nevertheless portends a fractured future.

In Bear Grease, the fracture becomes more of a chasm – literally and figuratively.  1950’s America was anything but idyllic for indigenous peoples.  The irony of kids whose ancestors were forced to into horrible ‘boarding schools’ , suffering much mistreatment there, putting on a show that revels in poodle skirts and ponytails is not lost on anyone.   So I wonder, why this show?  Is it to reclaim emotional territory, satirizing an already frivolous satire with joy and silliness?  Is it a reinterpretation? A revolution?  Examining the amalgam thus created is part of what makes Bear Grease interesting.

The piece has an awkward, ‘let’s put on a show’ vibe.  The cast brings a variety of skill sets and skill levels to the stage.  Director /writer Crystle Lightning has loaded the piece with content referencing life on the Reservation, as well as backstage intrigue to rival onstage chemistry.  The production also combines film and animation with the IRL action.  The lack of focus results in a show that is unpolished and inconsistent, however much heart the cast pour into it.  I must note that some of the backstage humor is so blue I could not recommend Bear Grease for viewing by children.  I found the vulgarity very out of place.

Nevertheless, the show is fun.  The animations are delightful, as are the ‘candid’ backstage filmed interviews, which make up part of the pre-show.  Excellent costumes combine traditional indigenous elements and accessories with 1950’s style.  The girls’ dresses are delightfully colorful and voluminous.  One of my favorite moments is the rap Henry Cloud Andrade improvised at the top of the show.  It was impressive and funny, and it drew the audience right in.  I wish that focus could prevail throughout the performance.  Alas, the disjointedness, as well some lighting and sound issues, kept us at arm’s length.

This is black box theater, so we have to accept some technical difficulties.  In many scenes actors in the background basically perform in shadow.  Some of the more glamorous lighting effects are more effective, when the actors hit their marks.   A row of girls in emerald green dresses and gloves in individual spotlights made for a great visual in the opening number.  Two significant sound issues also need to be addressed:  an overly loud musical track drowning out onstage singing, and inconsistent effectiveness of body mics,  which are too far forward on the actors’ faces.  It is normal practice to tape the mics to the forehead or just over the ear.

Bear Grease particularly shines when highlighting indigenous culture.  They would be wise to refocus in that direction.  If you’re going to be niche, be that niche.  Ditch the backstage dirty jokes and give more space for the material where indigenous and musical theater voices combine.  Tammy Rae Lamouche as Rezzo singing “Stand By Me” in Cree was something special.  Bryce Morin as Danny performing a drum dance was captivating.  That’s the magic.  That’s the show.

Bear Grease, written and directed by LightningCloud (Crystle Lightning and Henry Cloud Andrade)

With Melody McArthur, Bryce Morin, Tammy Rae Lamouche, Rodney McLeod, Nipîy Iskwew, Justin Giehm, Raven Bright, Haley Robinson, Mikey Harris, Alyssa Trujillo & Crystle Lightning.

Video Production by Dustin “Birdie” Vince, costume design by Nipîy Iskwew, lighting design by Jeremy (Ill Wero) Echols

Opens June 20th at the St. Luke’s Theatre (308 West 46th St.   For tickets or go to: www.beargreaselive.com.  Run Time: 2 hours with one 15 minute intermission.

yoast_head_json.description: Bear Grease.  It's a musical theater / night club act / low comedy / video show all jumbled into  one.  It has some really fun, but it’s overly ambitious, disorganized and definitely niche. Co-created in Treaty 6 Territory in Alberta (Canada) by husband and wife writing team LightningCloud (Crystle Lightning and Henry Cloud Andrade),  Bear Grease weaves elements of native cultures from various indigenous nations, including Enoch Cree Nation, Beaver First Nation, Big Stone Cree Nation and others into the narrative of the popular musical Grease, adding an indigenous ‘voice’ to an American musical theater classic.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Prince Faggot is a beguiling tragicomedy.  “Beguiling” – I don’t often use that word, but it is the one that surfaced. Jordan Tannahill‘s play is a dense tapestry of wonder, imagination, sexuality, humor and stinging observation.

That’s just for starters.

The press release tells us that this company is an ensemble of queer and trans performers who have been released into the imagination of Mr. Tannahill who has chosen to imagine the Royal Family (yeah THAT one) dealing with Prince George’s homosexuality.  You thought Meghan was a Royal fly in the ointment?  Queer George would be a tornado.

What is beguiling is that we are cordially invited to observe privacies and intimate moments on both sides of this tale.  The Royals are nothing if not cordial.  Mr. Tannahill is Canadian, and this may have influenced his knowledge of the details of Royal life.  His time as a fetish sex worker (see the program bio) may have influenced his take on the Prince’s sexual activity.  Table settings and posture and so forth are placed against the rituals of queer and trans life.  It is an even match.

No matter your sexual persuasion or preferences, it is a given that there is room for all of us in the observation deck.

At the center of the tale is the love story between George (Performer 6/John McCrea) and Dev (Performer 1/Mihir Kumar) who is a college chum of George’s and a first generation Indian.  He is the Brown subject of his lover, the future King, and he knows it sometimes more than George himself.  We begin in 2032 when George is old enough to bring a romantic interest home to meet the folks.  A lot has changed in the world out there.  Within the Royal Family, however, not so much.  As we watch, it is Dev who appears to see the larger picture operating and has found pockets where he can still breathe   It is George who finds himself caught in limbo.

We are told right from the start that this is a fabulation.  It is a made up story based on the question that IF George were queer, what kind of a life would he be allowed to have.  Especially if his beloved were Brown.

This story is told with sensitivity so dear it makes you hold your breath for fear of breaking the spell.  The backdrop is a panoply of lacerating paper cuts that move at the speed of light.  Just when you think you have grabbed onto an idea you discover that it has slipped by and been replaced with another idea traveling just as fast.  There are also moments interspersed with the story line in which actors appear to step out from behind the veil of their characters and connect with us in the present.

This is a rich ensemble.  Rich in talent and rich in generosity toward one another and to us.  Chowdhury’s direction is seamless.  The action is deceptive because it is choreography on so many levels.  The scene changes are more akin to hand-offs in a relay.  And no one drops the baton.  Mention must be made of the many characters that almost every performer takes on with what can only be called raw glee.

Don’t let the title, “Prince Faggot”, put you off.  Fasten your seatbelts and open your mind.  You will be surprised at how much new information you can stuff into that noggin of yours.

Bravo all around.  Wish I had more than 5 stars to play with here.

Jordan Tannahill’s Prince Faggot, directed by Shayok Misha Chowdhury

WITH Rachel Crowl, K. Todd Freeman, David Greenspan, Mihir Kumar, John McCrea, and N’yomi Allure Stewart

David Zinn (Scenic Designer), Montana Levi Blanco (Costume Designer), Isabella Byrd (Lighting Designer), Lee Kinney (Sound Design & Original Music), Cookie Jordan (Wig and Hair Designer), Sarah Lunnie (Dramaturg), UnkleDave’s Fight-House (Intimacy Coordination)

Co-produced by Playwrights and Soho Rep, in association with Jeremy O. Harris and Josh Godrey of bb².

Through July13 at Playwrights Horizons.  Tickets HERE

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

What is the truth of war? The bottom line of it? People, average, everyday humans kill other average, everyday humans for a belief, a cause, a hope for a better world. That, better, of course, is always subjective, based on the wants and beliefs of the side you are on.

The belief that particular members of the world are inferior, that a certain political stance overrides another. Often, the beliefs center on racism, sexism, and separatism of the other. The other being those who do not share your skin color, your beliefs, your religion, secular or spiritual, your political beliefs, or your sexual orientation.

It is 1937,  Madrid and the rest of Spain are hanging by a thread. The government is a fascist platform and it is exterminating, eliminating those who do not follow form. The opposing force making a last stand in Madrid, the Spanish Republic, is doing what it can to fight the Fascist backed by Italy and Nazi Germany, but they are far too small and lack the strength of weaponry to succeed. In comes the cavalry, volunteers from all over the world to help fight the Fascists. Average everyday folks who stand by a Communist belief that we are all created equal and deserve equal treatment. That there should no longer be exploitation of labor, that communities are all comrades in class. None are considered higher and none lower. All humans should be equal in the eyes of the government. Desiring to create a form of living bliss where all are viewed with the same respect and care by the government.

Photo By Pablo Calderon-Santiago

These believers traveled from around the world to another country, most of whom did not speak the language, to help that country defeat the Fascists and achieve communist bliss. This is the story told by the theatrical company, What Will The Neighbors Say? in their newest endeavor, At The Barricades, now playing at MITU580. “At The Barricades”, beautifully directed by Frederica Borlenghi, is a 100-minute reflective narrative delving into the minds and hearts of those who volunteered their time, and for many, lost their lives to a cause that was not a part of their everyday existence. They traveled by ships and any means possible to get to Spain to try and make a difference.

The American volunteers, men and women, white and black, were fighting alongside their Spanish comrades and were known as The Abraham Lincoln Brigade. This is their story and the story of the Spaniards, the Scottish, and so many others from all over the world who fought, worked, and died together to defeat fascism, to stop the tyrannical dictator Francisco Franco Bahamonde.

The play reaches back in time and asks those who fought, “What is your story?” It is riveting. The actors are all living their characters. We are caught up in the battle, in the mundane of daily life, in the constant need to lift each other with the understanding that their presence matters. They are helping the people of Spain. “Better to die standing than to live on your knees.” But it is not all fighting and pondering; there is dancing and laughter. We humans will always look for the rainbow when we can, reminding ourselves of the beauty of life.

The cast of six is a tight, marvelous ensemble. They are seamless in their depictions. Writers James Clements and Sam Hood Adrain have captured the stories, dreams, and voices that reshaped a country, embracing and lifting all of its inhabitants.

Please note: The show contains flashing lights, atmospherics, and gunshots/explosions.

What Will the Neighbors Say? presents At the Barricades
Written by James Clements & Sam Hood Adrain Directed by Federica Borlenghi
World Premiere
Cast: Sam Hood Adrain,  Stephanie Del Bino, James Clements, Edu Díaz, Devante Lawrence, and Chelsie Sutherland

Creative Team:  Set Design by Frank J. Oliva, Costume Design by Johanna Pan, Sound Design by Stephanie Carlin, and Lighting Design by Adrian Yuen, with Stage Management and Script Supervision by Skye Pallo Ross.

Running Time: 100 minutes with no intermission

At The Barricades playing June 12-29

MITU580 – 580 Sackett St Unit A – Ground Fl, Brooklyn, NY 11217

content.rendered:
By Vicki Weisfeld

Two River Theater in Red Bank, New Jersey, opened an ambitious production of Arthur Miller’s award-winning The Price last weekend, directed by Brandon J. Dirden and running through June 29. Don’t miss this opportunity to see this compelling production of one of Miller’s most thought-provoking plays.

NYPD sergeant Victor Franz (played by Kevin Isola) is eligible for retirement, but hesitating to make that change. Yet profound changes loom. The Manhattan brownstone where his family possessions are stored is being torn down, and he must deal with an attic crammed full of furniture and, more important, memories. His wife Esther (Andrea Syglowski) wants him to sell this collection for as much as possible, because she believes they’ve lived a too-Spartan existence for too long. Into their lives comes a wily octogenarian appraiser, Gregory Solomon (Peter Van Wagner), bent on talking Victor into a much less lucrative deal.

Who owns all this stuff?, Solomon asks. Actually, ownership is shared by Victor and his estranged older brother Walter, a successful physician. Walter isn’t answering Victor’s phone calls, so with the wrecking ball on the way, the responsibility appears to be Victor’s by default. After a lengthy roundabout negotiation, Victor finally agrees to Solomon’s terms. At the end of Act I, in the midst of Solomon’s counting out the agreed-upon payment, Walter (Karl Kenzler) unexpectedly appears, the proverbial fly in the ointment.

When the Depression hit, the upper middle class Franz family—chauffeur and all (like Miller’s own family)—vanished overnight, and Victor and his recently widowed father retreated to the attic of their building. With little financial help from his brother, he had to keep his father alive. “We were eating garbage here,” he says, and can’t let go of it.

Is Walter the selfish brother who denied Victor the money he needed to finish college, where he was a promising science student? Victor has thought so for decades. But as old grievances are revisited and secrets emerge, one after another, your impression of the brothers—their mistakes, their blind spots, their lost possibilities, and the high price of memory—is repeatedly reevaluated.

As in other Arthur Miller plays, there’s a lot of talking, a lot of arguing, a lot of lines to learn! The cast makes lightning-fast adjustments as, surrounded by reminders of the family’s past, the mood constantly shifts. Van Wagner, as Solomon, is alternately comic, tragic, and maddening. Perfect. Walter and Esther make profound reevaluations of their situations, while embittered Victor, with the most to lose, seems unable to move on, though, maybe . . .

Production credits to Neil Prince (scenic designer), Karen Perry (costumes), Driscoll Otto (lighting), Germán Martínez (sound), Cici Campbell (wig, hair, and makeup), and Jason Yeager (composer).

Two River theater is located at 21 Bridge Avenue, Red Bank, off Exit 109 on the Garden State Parkway, and a short walk from New Jersey Transit’s North Jersey Coast Rail Line. For tickets, call the box office at 732-345-1400 or visit the Box Office online. Through June 29.

content.rendered:
By Victoria Lynne Dammer

Any day of the year, you can read stories about the rise and fall of Hollywood actors. Alcohol, drugs, and messed up relationships with lovers and directors are just a sample of the struggles in theatrical life. Don’t forget the internal struggles we all have as humans.

So, writer, actor, and director Thomas G. Waites brought his happiness, pain, and redemption to the stage in Lucky Man, A Warrior’s Journey at the Gene Frankel Theatre.

His guitar and the three-piece band Heartbreak Waites accompanied him as he expressed his pain and glory through words and song. The performance resonates with the audience’s soul through this personal journey that some of us have experienced.

Waites had early success, starring as the scout Fox character in the 1979 action thriller The Warriors. But the director fired him, removing his name from the credits. A cult classic, the franchise spun off video games and a comic book series. Fortunately, Waites said he received payment and gained international recognition. He remarked he was still receiving dividends from his performance in the movie.

In 1979, Waites had another supporting role in And Justice For All alongside Al Pacino. He didn’t get fired, and his credits were on the movie site. Waites improvised an impressive impression of Pacino and shared he received the nickname “One Time Tommy” for his talent to perform his lines in one take, much to the director’s delight and budget.

In 1982, Waites had a supporting role in John Carpenter’s successful horror film, The Thing. Just like The Warriors, the movie has become a cult classic, thanks to Carpenter’s genius and his willingness to delve into the horror genre.

Waites’ life went into the abyss after his performance with Carpenter. Waites said, “It (The Thing) was one moment that will alter the course of your life forever.” The movie certainly did that for the audience who followed it.

As painful as it was, Waites shared his domestic uncoupling and his eventual reconciliation with the wife he loved and then unloved. Alcohol ruined most of his life, and finally, being sober enhanced his life.

Waites shared his insight that all should embrace.

“I ought to write a book about Hollywood–‘What not to do by Thomas G Waites.”’

After this performance, it will be a bestseller.

See this engaging performance. It will pull you in. You will rejoice in redemption. You will believe in second chances.

John Goodman and Evan Azriliant present Lucky Man, written and performed by Thomas G. Waites. Featuring music by the band Heartbreak Waites. Directed by Joe Danisi. Press by  JT-PR A limited engagement at the Gene Frankel Theatre through June 22.

content.rendered:
Romeo, come forth; come forth, thou fearful man:

Affliction is enamour’d of thy parts,

And thou art wedded to calamity.

This reinterpretation of Romeo and Juliet, which ran at the Sheen Center, featured a largely Asian cast as the feuding Montagues and Capulets in a supposedly “dystopian” setting shaped by “fate, class conflict, and astrology,” according to the program notes.

Under the vision of artistic directors Venkatesh Vohra and Emily Nunes, who play Romeo and Juliet respectively, the production incorporated some appealing elements for modern audiences of the Bard’s classic tale. The ambient interludes by Ana Roxane lent a feeling of mysticism to the show, underscored by the regular appearance of four chorus members (Melody Khamp, Paris Dwyer, Sana Bokhari, and BinBin Kuo) who dance around and encircle the ill-fated characters. The costumes by Freia Koppmann were another highlight, which included stylish, East and South Asian-inspired outfits for the young lovers that would not be out of place at a Bushwick bar. The adults, including Lady Capulet (Amy Frances Quint), Lord Montague (Anuj Parikh), and Juliet’s Nurse (Debra Nguyen), all wore imposing, dark-colored outfits that draped to the floor and added a sense of funerary foreboding. In terms of performances, Venkatesh Vohra was a pitch-perfect Romeo and Jonathan Morgan was a rollicking Mercutio, with both actors nailing the cross between sincerity and goofy boyishness. Debra Nguyen also shone as the pious, yet meddling Nurse.

Occasionally, the artistic choices felt out of sync with any larger design for the production. While the show notes claimed that the show depicted a dystopia ruled by “wealth, secrecy, and surveillance,” it was difficult to get a cohesive sense of this particular Verona. The only set piece was a balcony with South Asian or Middle Eastern patterning on it that did not connect to almost any other element of the production. The young Capulets and Montagues wore school uniforms with long ties when they were not dressed in contemporary clothing. Visually, it felt like there was little to unite the Montagues or Capulets, other than the fact that the Capulets were mostly played by white actors and the Montagues were mostly Asian. However, the play did not choose to focus much on racial divisiveness, either, so that distinction felt relatively unimportant. When Romeo stabbed Tybalt, modern American police siren noises were heard as blue and red flashing lights went off. Some of the acting felt distracting as well, with Tybalt crying out “ay yai yai” when he was struck (twice). The time and place felt ambiguous despite attempts to center the show. The aforementioned chorus added a bit of color to the world, playing ping pong in the background and appearing to gossip on the steps, but it did not add to any particular themes or setting of the play.

Interestingly, the most conscious decision-making seemed centered on Friar Laurence, played exceptionally by Wayne Yeh. This Friar Laurence is a monk who does movements reminiscent of qigong and yoga. He carries a gravitas and generally peaceable demeanor that easily convinces Romeo and Juliet to confide in him, despite his eventual hand in their destruction. The chorus appears in two of his scenes, once in his initial monologue about vices and virtues, and later as he explains his plan to put Juliet into a false-death. The chorus encircles the Friar during his monologue, creating a heightened sense of drama and mysticism to his speech about the potential for good and evil in all living beings. While many characters could be said to play a pivotal role in the fate of Romeo and Juliet, this production focuses its attention on the Friar, placing an emphasis not necessarily on surveillance or wealth, but on spirituality, morality, and faith.

As this is the No Theatre Company’s debut production, it is clear that they have all the talent necessary to create engaging and thought-provoking theatre. I look forward to seeing how they bring these elements together more cohesively in the future.

ROMEO + JULIET– Written by William Shakespeare, Artistic Direction by Venkatesh Vohra and Emily Nunes, Performance Direction by Emily Allan

WITH: Venkatesh Vohra (Romeo), Emily Nunes (Juliet), Amy Frances Quint (Lady Capulet), Debra Nguyen (Nurse), Wayne Yeh (Friar Laurence), Sashank Gummella (Prince Escalus), Jonathan Morgan (Mercutio), Ameer Ali (Benvolio), Ati Oppelt (Paris), Marco Villard (Tybalt), Anuj Parikh (Lord Montague)

Set by Cherisse Elizaga Gray & Edwin Lam; costumes by Freia Koppmann; original score by Ana Roxanne, choreography by Alvin Tran

At Sheen Center for Thought and Culture, (212) 219-3132 , https://www.sheencenter.org/, June 12-15, 2025. Run time: 2 hours and 45 minutes (includes 15 minute intermission).
